speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, February 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government; and the amendment of Mr. Gray (Windsor West) (p. 17722).

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to express my pleasure that I have an opportunity to rise today to speak on the hon. Minister of Finance's most recent budget, a budget which comes closer to addressing the needs and expressed desires of Canadians than any other budget which I have seen before this House.
There has been one very clear message which I have received as a politician during the course of the last few years, and particularly during the course of the last 12 months. A frequently expressed desire on the part of my constituents, and I believe other Canadians, is that the Government of Canada must show leadership and take the necessary steps to start to address the problem of the national debt and the annual deficit.
Canada's national debt is now reaching the total of some $400 billion. I suspect that many of us live in a world where the magnitude of $400 billion is not entirely clear to us. When you think in terms of $400 billion meaning a debt of some $13,000 or more per capita, I think that figure becomes more comprehensible for us as Canadians.
When I speak to people of all ages, I find a veiy broad consensus on the fact that that the problem of the debt is one which is starting to worry and, in some cases, starting to almost terrify some Canadians.
When I speak to senior citizens or when I am in discussion with grandparents, they often raise the question of the debt and what the implications will be for their grandchildren. In fact, I find that many senior citizens-and I know that their economic circumstances are somewhat at variance with others-are saying: "We are enjoying many benefits today which we have not previously enjoyed in life."
I have had some senior citizens say to me that they are better off in economic terms than they have ever been before in their life. That is not to suggest for a moment that all senior citizens fall into that category.
What they go on to say is the fact that they are concerned for their children, and particularly for their grandchildren.
To some degree, I suppose, their abhorrence of debt is a reflection of the fact that they lived during the 1930s. They were parents during the 1930s and had the responsibility of trying to raise others at a time when there was immense depression in Canada and elsewhere throughout the world.
One of the by-products of the 1930s for many people who lived through it was the determination that they would never ever again become the victim of being in debt because they realized how vulnerable they were in that situation.
I come from western Canada. Part of the tragedy of the 1930s was not only the loss of jobs but the loss of farmland which occurred. A real crisis developed due to the fact that people who were in debt could not meet their obligations.
Their generation, particularly, is dismayed by the policies of government at all levels, which originated in the 1970s and into the 1980s, where we began to spend money which we did not have.
It is ironic that we began to spend money at a time when we did not need to spend money.

March 1, 1991
The Budget
In any event, we have a legacy today, a legacy of debt which we are leaving to future generations, of almost $400 billion. Each of us in this Chamber understands that that figure must continue to grow because of the interest on the debt. We have a situation today where the interest on the accumulated debt is now some $43 billion.
Although we have been able to make progress as a government, since 1984, in having a balance in our favour, in terms of operating costs, that debt, which is a burden, a millstone around the necks of all Canadians, means that the debt continues to grow each year because of the interest on it.
What I see in this budget is a determined effort by the Minister of Finance and his colleagues to address the question of the annual deficit. When that is addressed we will be in a position to address the issue of the national debt itself.
I sense from the reports which I have had from my constituency and conversations which I have had with my constituents that this budget, quite frankly, is being received better than any other budget that we have brought down since we came to power in 1984. One of the reasons for this is that we are focusing less on spending and more on saving.
One of the ironies of being a politician, when you come to meet with your own newspaper people after a budget, is that veiy frequently the question which they ask is: What is in this budget for this constituency? In this case, what is in this budget for Brandon-Souris?
The interesting thing about that question is that there is an implication that no budget can be relevant to my constituency, or perhaps to any other constituency in Canada, unless it is a spending budget which is bringing them dollars from the Government of Canada, i.e. from the people of Canada. The interesting thing this time is that I did not hear that question being asked as frequently as I have in the past. I think there is a very broad consensus, including among the journalists of Canada, that we are at a crisis point and we must continue to save.
A second theme which I heard frequently throughout this year was that the federal government must show leadership and must begin to get its own act in order. I suggest that we have made some progress in that regard.
For example, there are now 12,000 fewer civil service positions than there were in 1984. There are many people in my constituency who are pleased by that, because they believe that government has grown larger than they, as Canadians, can afford.
They have been saying in the province of Manitoba, and certainly in the constituency of Brandon-Souris, that we must show leadership by ensuring that some caps and restraints are put in place on these huge federal-public expenditure programs, of which we are a part.
I believe the decision of the federal government to ensure, for example, that there will be regulations on spending during the course of the next five years, regulations put in place by law, will be well received. I believe that the decision to cap civil service salary increases by 3 per cent will be well received by the majority of my constituents-not by all of my constituents, of course. I believe the fact that the cabinet will take a freeze in salary for the upcoming year will be well received. I believe the fact that the salaries of members of Parliament and senators are to be more tightly constrained will be well received.
I believe that most Canadians will understand that we are in fact trying to place our own house in order and they will understand, therefore, that we can quite rightly turn to the provinces and to other levels of government and encourage them to accept our leadership as well.
Another issue which I heard a great deal about this year was the GST. I have spoken in the House before about a meeting I had in my constituency at which those present indicated in no uncertain fashion their displeasure with the GST.
Having said that, a second part of their message to me then and later was the fact that they would find the GST to be a more tolerable tax if they were certain the revenues would not be used to fund new government programs. They were afraid that any additional revenue that might be derived from the GST would go to create new programs, which has characterized government spending since the beginning of the 1970s.
The fact that GST revenues will be directed toward a deficit reduction fund will be very well received in my constituency. The fact that the resources from privatization will be directed toward such a fund will be well
March 1, 1991

received in my constituency. The fact that Canadians, if they wish, can make direct contributions to such a deficit reduction fund will be well received in my constituency. The fact that there may therefore be, once the economy turns around, more revenue from this particular tax than we might have anticipated will also be more acceptable to my constituents because it will be directed specifically toward deficit reduction.
The question of transfer payments is, of course, important to the province of Manitoba as it is to many other provinces. I would like to spend a few moments looking at that, if I may.
I come from a constituency and a province in which we have depended to a very substantial degree on transfer payments. In fact, some recent research which has come to light indicates that Manitobans on a per capita basis have benefited more significantly from the transfer payments and from the federal government's sharing of moneys than have citizens of other provinces, somewhat to the surprise of my own constituents.
It is important to understand that the transfer payments to the province of Manitoba, as they will to many other provinces, will increase with this budget as they have done with previous budgets. Not to the extent that our friends in the provincial government would wish, because they are obviously anxious to receive as much revenue from outside their own jurisdiction as they can. Transfer payments will increase to the province and the Government of Manitoba, according to my calculations, by 3.1 per cent. I think it is important to stress the fact that there will be an increase because there are so many people who talk in terms of "reductions in".
There is an assumption, therefore, when you read only the headline, as many people are inclined to do, that provincial governments, including the government of Manitoba, will be receiving less money in the future than they received in the past. That is not the case. Indeed, they will receive more money in the coming fiscal year than they received in the current or the previous fiscal year.
According to my calculations, Manitobans will receive $1,720 per person in the form of transfer payments from the Government of Canada and that constitutes a very
The Budget
significant part of their budget, somewhere in the vicinity of 37 or 38 per cent, if I recall correctly.
I also want to make it clear that there has been an immense amount of concern in my province, as in other provinces, with respect to the needs of agriculture, and I represent an agricultural constituency. When I say that, I include the city of Brandon in that definition, because certainly the business community in Brandon is exceedingly dependent upon agriculture. We are living in very, very difficult times in the field of agriculture.
As I stand here, I am proud that I can say to my constituents and to this House that support for agriculture has been and continues to be a very obvious priority for the Government of Canada. In fact, our support has increased-

speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend say it is nonsense. If he will check his statistics he will understand, perhaps, more clearly than he does now that our support for agriculture has increased by some 500 per cent in terms of direct payments to farmers since we came to power in 1984. My constituents understand that, even if my hon. friend who represents the constituency of Kingston and the Islands does not. In this budget there is an additional $1.3 billion for agriculture. At a time when the government is cutting back in other areas, it is continuing to provide more money for agriculture. It may indeed not be enough. There is money in the reserves within the estimates and I would suspect that we as a government will have to make use of some of those reserves to assist with some sort of additional form of assistance to agriculture.
In the meantime, we in this budget are providing the funds necessary to support two exceedingly important agricultural stabilization programs, the program which we know in the west as GRIP and the program which we know in the west as NISA.
Unfortunately, in the province of Manitoba, the government has not yet decided under what circumstances it will participate in the GRIP program and it has indicated that it unfortunately does not believe that it can financially participate in the NISA program. If indeed that is their decision this year, I will regret it but I would hope

March 1, 1991
The Budget
that the government will be able to participate next year; that it will understand the importance of doing so.
There is also in this budget new financial assistance for the disabled. I would like to mention in passing that I am particularly pleased to see that not only because the disabled of Canada have some very special needs that often go unrecognized, but particularly because as I stand in this House today I am conscious of the fact that I am the successor to the Hon. Walter Dinsdale who served this House for some 31 years and who throughout that entire career demonstrated a very strong commitment to the disabled. I know that if he were here today, he would be very pleased to see the provisions in this budget which would help meet the needs of that particular constituency.
I am also conscious of the fact that in this budget there is additional spending, perhaps more additional spending than some of my constituents would prefer. There is additional spending to assist with the needs of the unemployed. We are conscious of the fact that we are in a recession. The newspapers seem to suggest to some degree that this recession is worse in Ontario and perhaps in Quebec than it is in the west. I personally would differ with that on the grounds that the recession came to the west in my mind before it came to the eastern part of Canada. However, things that happen in the west are not always as well noted by the media of Canada, unfortunately. Nevertheless, the reality of the recession is there and there are some provisions to try to assist with that.
I think that the most important theme within this budget is the theme that suggests that we as a government understand that Canada can go only so far down that very slippery road to massive debt. There is also a theme within this budget that if we are to address the problems of that debt, there are no easy ways of doing so.
I think that is worth noting because I am afraid there is a certain inclination with some of my constituents and undoubtedly with other Canadians to assume that there is some sort of easy solution to the reduction of the deficit and to the abolition of the debt. I dare say that any of us, as members of Parliament, or any of those who are watching, could probably create their own wish list of what could be abolished, what programs could be cancelled and where we could save money. I would think that most of us could identify $1 billion in savings that we would gladly put in place.
With human nature being what it is, that $1 billion saving that we would come forth with would probably not include many programs, perhaps not include any programs, which would impact upon us as individuals because there is obviously a human tendency to want to make savings at the expense of someone else, someone perhaps of a different class, someone who works in a different profession, someone who lives in a different city, someone who lives in a different provinces or a different region. The reality as we well know is the fact that we cannot easily reduce the deficit, which will be some $30 billion this year. We cannot do that in such a way that does not impact upon us as individuals.
I am reminded as I speak of certain reductions and savings which we have made in the past. I am reminded, for example, of the fact that we proposed in a previous budget to reduce the subsidies to VIA by some $300 million over an extended period of time. We did that because the required subsidies for VIA were going out of sight; $600 million with the evidence indicating that the subsidies would eventually reach $1 billion per year.
When we did reduce those subsidies we heard very quickly from those who would be directly impacted by it and even from many who had not made use of VIA for a long, long time. One of my most vociferous critics on the question of the reduction of VIA subsidies mentioned to me once in passing that he had not been on the train for seven years. I guess the message there is that if we are going to reduce subsidies to VIA or if we are going to reduce subsidies in any other given program, it is going to impact upon us wherever we live.
There are no easy ways to reduce the deficit. Surely if we are honest with each other we would understand if there were an easy way to reduce the deficit and reduce the national debt, governments would have found it in the past.
What we are asking now in this budget is that Canadians realize first of all that we are committed to the task of deficit reduction and, second, that we are prepared to provide leadership ourselves and, having done so, we can rightly call upon other Canadians to follow in that example.
March 1, 1991

This debate and this budget are about more than just the next fiscal year. This budget is about the directions Canada will follow in the next decade. That is why this budget, in my mind, may well be a bell-wether for budgets to come.
What we are saying to the people of Canada is that we currently must take 35 cents out of every dollar of the tax revenues which we receive in order to service the debt. We can no longer afford to do so and we must ask others to join with us in ensuring that this budget in fact is a beginning of what I hope will be a crusade to attack the deficit and eventually to reduce the national debt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I also represent an area, as does the hon. member, that depends largely on transfer payments. He mentioned that there is no easy way to reduce the deficit and I agree.
I would just like to ask the hon. member for Brandon-Souris some questions in terms of how this government is trying to reduce the deficit. Why is it trying to reduce the deficit on the backs of Canadians who may not necessarily have the resources to succeed as much as other Canadians? I am talking about the $100 million which is what I believe has been cut from the Canadian Jobs Strategy, some cuts in the Canada Assistance Program, some cuts in the native programming, or outright elimination of some native programming, cuts in the CBC programming, and cuts in what I consdier a very important area, the environmental green plan, which would have tried to do something about the pollution that is occurring in the north not because it is our fault, but because international forces are creating pollution in the region.
If we are going to be environmentally conscious in the future, I am wondering why we are cutting back on the environmental spending? Those are the questions I would just like to ask, as well as some others about other services that have been cut such as the Postal Services Assistance Program for the north.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my thanks to the hon. member for his series of questions, because he has introduced several themes that I think are important to address.
The Budget
Perhaps I might begin by dealing with them in reverse order, if I may. He refers to the environment and, I think, if I heard him correctly, he talked about cuts in spending on the environment. The reality is, as the minister indicated in the House yesterday, this government is providing an additional 20 per cent to 25 per cent to the Department of the Environment to be used during the up-coming fiscal year. There is no reduction in spending for the Department of the Environment, in fact it is just the very opposite.
First of all, in the estimates tabled yesterday, there is an increase of 4.7 per cent to the department itself, and there is an additional $250 million being provided under the green plan.
When the hon. member made his comments, I think he was referring to the fact that the green plan is being extended from some five years to six years. That is true, but what is important to understand is that the entire objective of the green plan remains intact. All of the strategy within the green plan remains intact. We will, for example, still plant 325 million trees, but we will plant 325 million trees over six years instead of over five years.
When speaking of the green plan, I think it is important to remember that this is the only government in Canadian history that has ever developed any long-term strategy for the environment. This is the only government in Canadian history that has ever put in place a long-term-in this case now six years-spending program for the environment.
While we might differ on what should be in that program or how rich it should be, the significance in that accomplishment should not be lost by either the House or Canadians in general.
The hon. member refers to the CBC in terms of reductions and spending for the CBC. One of the things that I sometimes discuss with my constituents is the fact that we, as a government, as a country, must have priorities in spending just as we as families must have priorities in spending. None of us in our own family situation or, I suspect, none of us who are members of Parliament at least, can afford to do everything within the family that we would wish to do, nor can we afford to do everything for the family that we would wish to do. Government is really no different than that.

The Budget
I guess what I would say in return to the hon. member is that when the time comes to establish priorities, we must again make some tough decisions, decisions that will not necessarily be popular in all parts of the country, nor are they necessarily the decisions which would be made by each and every Canadian. I look at this budget and I see certain reductions in place.
The hon. member has mentioned the CBC. Let me mention the proposed cultural research centre for the city of Montreal or the proposed expenditure of $88 million on the ballet centre in Toronto, and the cultural centre that was proposed for Edmonton. I can appreciate that each of these proposed programs has merit, and I can appreciate as well how they are important, particularly to the people who would be directly served by them. However, I would also suggest to the hon. member that the vast majority of my constituents, but not all, would place some of these proposed expenditures on a lower priority. They would give them a lower priority than others would. I think they will understand, therefore, how we cannot provide each and every proposal with the kind of dollars they would wish.
With respect to the Canadian Assistance Program, I think it is important to understand that those provinces, such as the province of Manitoba, which receive transfer payments will be as fully funded under CAP as they were in the past. Yes, transfer payments under the EPF, the Established Programs Funding, are frozen, but not under the Canada Assistance Program.
With respect to the Canadian Jobs Strategy, I, for one, am pleased by the innovation which I have seen in the Canadian Jobs Strategy but there are many who were very sceptical of it, including some in my own community who traditionally provided some of these training programs at community colleges.
I think, by and large, the money which has been spent has been useful. For one thing it has provided more flexibility than we have had in the past. So I like the strategy. I also understand that we have not fully utilized some of the moneys in the past so I gather there is some flexibility in that regard.
Finally, with regard to the ability to pay, the question of transfer payments. This is a major issue in my province. I would like to remind the provinces that the government requires 35 cents of every tax dollar to
service the debt. They, on average, only require 12 cents of their revenue dollar to service their debt. Those figures in themselves suggest to me in terms of ability to pay that we have less manoeuvrability and less flexibility because of the debt and the cost of servicing that debt than do our provincial colleagues.
We are not asking them to do anything more than we are willing to do ourselves. But we are asking them to share in the task of dealing with the burden of the national debt because it is a national problem. It is not just a problem of this government. It is not just a problem of this Parliament. It is a problem for all of Canada, and the implications are real and will be severe for those who come after us.
It is easy for politicians to spend money. Normally when we spend money, the people who receive it are pleased, there is publicity, we are doing something, we are bringing something to them. We are at a sad state of affairs if we have reached the point in Canada when the only criteria for accomplishment, when it comes to measuring the history of a government, is the fact that it spent more money than previous governments.
That is not what is being asked of us. What is being asked of us now is that we accept the task of providing leadership, of making difficult decisions, sometimes even unpopular decisions and clearly we suffer as a result in terms of the public opinion polls. It is important to provide that leadership because the decisions which we are making today are not designed simply for our benefit as politicians or for this generation; they are designed for the benefit of future generations.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in compliance with your recent announcement, I will be using ten minutes of the time and sharing with another member of my caucus.
I should remind the House that I represent a rural constituency made up of farms, small towns and small cities. It is the kind of constituency that the Conservative Party has traditionally considered itself as speaking for. But, over the past seven or eight years that tradition has fallen apart very sadly.
Now when I go into small towns to meet with chambers of commerce and councils, I find that they are worried about what is happening to their post offices. One of the few federal profiles in each of these communities is the federal post office, now being closed in many communities, shifted over to being privatized or, in some instances, disappearing altogether.
Usually the second federal profile that occurs in my small communities is the RCMP. The federal government at this very moment is busy trying to push off more of the cost of financing the RCMP on to these local municipalities. While most economic analyses show that 30 per cent of what the RCMP do in those rural communities is looking after federal responsibilities, the federal government is saying that is too much for us to bear, let the provinces and the small towns and small cities look after it.
The end result for some of the small cities is that they are placed in an almost impossible situation. They are in the position of hiring a police force of their own of four or five people at a cheaper rate than what the federal
The Budget
government is asking them to pay for the RCMP. Now these people do not want to give up the national police force. They believe in it. They are proud of it. Yet this last symbol of federalism in rural Canada is being pulled away by an off-loading of costs by the federal government.
Last, the thing that all small communities take some pride in is their local weekly newspapers. Canada Post, through a directive from the federal government to show a profit, has now decided that they are going to increase very dramatically the postal rates on those small community newspapers. All of the weekly papers which ship beyond a 40-mile radius have huge increases in postal costs, 10 times, 11 times the amount that they are paying now is being asked. This puts a further burden on holding small communities together, particularly in the prairies where 40 miles is barely the area which they service with the closure of towns and the thinning out of the population.
This budget, when you listen to the government's side, is a budget that has not raised very many taxes, except for a tobacco tax. They claim that there has been no increase in cost to people, that this is a hold the line budget and that this is an effort to reduce expenditures and get at, if not the national debt, certainly the annual deficit.
When you look at what is being put forward, you can readily see that the deficit is really not being cut. It is still at $30.5 billion. It has been hovering around $30 billion for the last seven years. The national debt has increased to in the neighbourhood of $400 billion, which has more than doubled in the period of time that the Conservative Party has held power. However, when you start looking into the budget, you see that there are a lot of extra costs that taxpayers and ordinary people are going to have to bear with the continuation of the program that this government put in place over previous budgets.
I recall David Suzuki, in a different context, trying to explain how the environment was getting into big trouble. He said we are all like the frog that is put into a pan of water and the heat is put under it. It begins to get warm and the frog sits there and becomes so insensitive to the extra heat that eventually it cooks. That is, to some extent, what is happening to people in rural Canada with this increased and continuous pressure from the federal government to put more costs on to them.

March 1, 1991
The Budget
The costs that have been added this year, which are not mentioned in the budget but are there, are the increased amounts of taxes which people will have to pay because of a continuation of deindexing.
In the personal income tax system alone this affects people. Adding up the reduced purchasing power of the family allowance because of the continuation of deindexing, the continuation of the clawback on family allowances and old age security, the reduction in the buying power of the child tax credit maximums and the income thresholds, the reduction of the buying power of the income tax brackets that are established, the reductions in the buying power of the value of the tax credits for personal, age and the married and child credits, we can see that the combined measures of this particular program being continued for this year will cost each family in Canada about $300 per year, an increase in tax revenues of about $1 billion.
As well, we have increases to the unemployment insurance accounts. It is not called a tax increase but it is about a 25 per cent increase in the amount of deductions that will come off working peoples' cheques to pay their share of the unemployment insurance program and employers will pay an equivalent percentage increase. This is in spite of the government having just changed that legislation in recent months to make the unemployment insurance fund self-sustaining, meaning no tax dollars go into it directly. We just collect through levies.
We were assured at that time by the government that the levels that were set in that legislation would remain for at least three years. Less than six months later there is a 25 per cent increase. That comes out of peoples' pockets.
As well there is the off-loading of costs from the federal government to the provincial government. My time only allows me to go into a few of them, but in my province the off-loading of health costs and post-secondary education costs through the Established Programs Financing means that Saskatchewan will lose funding from the federal government of $348 million in health care dollars and $140 million in post-secondary education financing over the next five years. That means there is about $100 extra cost per man, woman and child in Saskatchewan this year. Added to the off-loading of
federal responsibility for farm programs on to the provinces and individuals, the result is a tremendous figure.
Saskatchewan will be participating in the GRIP program. That means their annual charges at the provincial taxpayer level will be about $200 million, which almost quadruples the amount that Saskatchewan spends on agriculture. The bill that the farmer is asked to pay, including increased costs for crop insurance and GRIP, will be somewhere between $1 billion over the next five years for the province and between $1.5 billion and $2 billion over the next five years for producers. Just in additional provincial taxes, if the province wants to maintain the barely adequate service that they now have in health care and post-secondary education, it will cost every man, woman and child in Saskatchewan an additional $300 per year, thanks to the actions of this government in this budget. To say it is not a budget that increases taxes is completely false.
The last thing I would like to refer to, because few people have mentioned it, is the government's bogus effort to control spending. The government is proposing to implement legislation that would limit the amount of spending that it can engage in for each of the next few years. If the government is interested in that, it would recognize that the buck stops there. No one on this side of the House can initiate spending.
No backbencher on the government side of the House can initiate spending. Only the Prime Minister and his inner cabinet can initiate spending, by getting a royal recommendation. If the government wants to control spending, it can be controlled right there. The legislation they are proposing has so many provisos for breaking the rules that essentially it remains the same rule that we have followed for 123 years in this country; namely, that the Prime Minister and his inner cabinet decide when expenditures shall take place. And passing a "no spending" law will not change that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to speak on this budget with a comment that will I follow up with what I have to say. This budget is mean spirited, vindictive, and Draconian. In fact, this budget reminds me of a book that I read a number of years ago when I was first entering the workforce, a book called The Iron Heel.
March 1, 1991

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, it was a
little longer ago than 1986.
When I read The Iron Heel, I could not believe that in the two countries in North America that I was most familiar with in those early days, Canada and the United States, the kinds of things that happened in that book could in fact happen to working people, to the citizens of our countries. And yet looking at this budget, The Iron Heel is in fact coming down on the necks of the men and women who make this country strong through their work.
This budget continues the Tory attack on social services and renews its attack on the workers of this country. The Liberals gave us six-and-five; this government is giving workers three-and-two. If we remember what happened under six-and-five, I suspect that three-and-two will create even further suffering in this country.
This government has singled out public sector workers in its attack. It has used the threat of legislation to renege on its obligations to bargain with its employees in good faith. This government threatens back to work legislation if workers in the public sector exercise their legal right, and legitimate right, to strike. It threatens workers with lay-off if they negotiate a wage increase.
The effect of this budget on public sector workers is that for every 1 per cent increase they negotiate, they will be faced with a lay-off of 2,000 colleagues. What would be the point in accepting a 1 per cent salary increase in one hand and accepting a pink slip in the other hand? What kind of an option is that at the bargaining table? What kind of a pre-emptive strike has the government introduced at a time when this very week it has arrived at the bargaining table with the Public Service Alliance to negotiate the next round?
This legislation has clearly singled out public sector workers for wage restraint. This government has told public sector workers that they, loyal servants or not of the country, of this government, of all of us, will carry the burden for the terrible economic policies that this government has continually introduced since 1984.
The Budget
It is also important to consider that, in addition to the attack on public sector workers, this government has singled out transfer payments to the provinces for further cuts. This means cuts to those on welfare, cuts to hospitals, and cuts to colleges and universities.
These cuts will mean further lay-offs of health-care workers, of social service workers, of education workers. It will mean reduced services. It will mean increased hardship.
The Tory-made recession has already thrown hundreds of thousands of workers on to the unemployment insurance system and into the social service system. This budget ensures that these workers will suffer more and carry the brunt of the costs of this recession. In fact, Mr. McCracken from the right-wing Informetrica estimates that this budget will cost an additional 68,000 jobs.
The finance minister has made much of the fact that there are no new direct taxes in this budget. What he fails to mention is that the GST has cut into the household budget of Canadians already. What he fails to mention is that increased UI premiums will cost workers more, after a promise during the debate on Bill C-21, the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, that there would be no increases.
What he fails to mention is that provincial governments will be forced to recoup shortfalls in transfer payments from individual taxpayers, yet again the very people this government is attacking under this budget.
The minister has forecast double-digit unemployment rates, up to 10 per cent this year and 9.8 per cent next year, yet, there is no money for job creation.
Recent Stats Canada data show an additional inflation rate of 6.8 per cent. This will mean family allowance and old age security payments will decrease in real terms as they are only partially indexed to inflation. Families and seniors will suffer. The threshold for the clawback of these payments will rise, capturing more and more needy Canadians in its claws.
Inflation alone will add $300 to the tax bill of average Canadians-this on top of the GST.
We see cuts to labour adjustment programs, especially those aimed at helping older workers. When a worker in this country is laid off between the age of 45 and 65, the chances of being re-employed at a level that will

March 1, 1991
maintain his or her existing lifestyle, is tremendously diminished. This government had the temerity to cut labour adjustment programs.
We see cuts to the Canadian Jobs Strategy, this only months after the minister for employment made much of the new money being directed for training. There is no new money. It is smoke and mirrors. There is a shift and they are shucking and jiving. There is no new money.
Contrary to what the Minister of Finance said, this budget is not about shared responsibility. It is not about sharing the burden for the recession. Sharing the burden does not mean letting the wealthy off the hook. Sharing the burden does not mean letting big business off the hook. Sharing means fairness and this budget is not about fairness. It is about punishing Canadian families for Tory mismanagement.
The most optimistic of us cannot help but see that this budget is an attempt to break the back of organized labour in the public sector. It directly attacks public sector workers.
Yesterday the President of the Treasury Board announced that his government will be legislating contracting out of public sector jobs. This will mean, in fact, violation of the existing collective agreement. Does this mean that the end of free collective bargaining is happening in the Public Service? Is the minister in fact telling Canadians that this government's signature on a contract means nothing? Has this government become so bankrupt that it has abandoned all principles?
In closing, I would like to say that if the finance minister is truly interested in the bottom line, there is no doubt at all that the bottom line would include an investment in Canadian workers and in their families, the very people who labour to pay for government services, people who are unemployed and want to be part of the growth and redevelopment of this country. They need the tools.

subsubtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this morning members of the Liberal caucus met with 20 unions, representing more than half a million workers in the federal and provincial public sectors, to discuss the inane measures announced earlier this week by the finance minister.
The Public Service Alliance of Canada has 140,000 employees out of a total of 165,000 members in a negotiating position with Treasury Board. The Professional Institute of the Public Service has 22,000 employees out of 25,000 members who have been without a contract since before September 1990 and 10,000 of those are employees who are in a legal strike position.
It is quite clear from these figures that this government waited for exactly the right moment to introduce wage controls. The government waited until the majority of its employees were in a negotiating position before attacking. The government took advantage of a vulnerable Public Service and is forcing its workers to fight each other.
It is also clear that this government has one goal in mind and one goal only, the complete dismantling of Public Service unions at the federal level.

Madam Speaker, I wish to thank all those who called and wrote, and all the people I met, who expressed their support for our Canadian troops and the government during the gulf crisis.
Thank you Rosemont, thank you Hochelaga-Maisonneuve!
March 1, 1991

Madam Speaker, yesterday the government cut $18 million from the cultural sector in Canada. This is a terrible loss. This government does not realize how important the arts are in increasing understanding among Canada's different cultures.
Last night I attended the Ottawa premiere of an outstanding aboriginal play, "Dry Lips Oughta Move to Kapuskasing", written by Tomson Highway, a Cree Indian from Manitoba.
The performance last night was in support of the Canadian Native Arts Foundation. This foundation was established by John Kim Bell, a Mohawk Indian, to assist native youth with artistic talent to achieve their dreams.
I commend the Canadian Native Arts Foundation, Tomson Highway, and all the native actors, including Graham Greene, for a superb performance.
Aboriginal artists are emerging as a major cultural force in this country. I encourage everyone to see this play. It is full of deep spiritual meaning. I urge the government to stop cutting and to assist and support aboriginal languages and cultures.

Madam Speaker, construction will start this year in Quebec on a new CANMET mining research laboratory, at a cost of $15 million over a period of 5 years. The laboratory, which will have access to the Dorval mine in Val-d'Or, will be used to test mining methods, procedures and equipment.
Thanks to the active involvement of representatives from the mining, economic and political community in the Val-d'Or area, and of course the tremendous work done by Benoit Bouchard, Jake Epp, CANMET officials and the Prime Minister of Canada, this laboratory will open its doors very shortly in Val-d'Or, Quebec.
Madam Speaker, since 1984, I have defended the Abitibi region in Ottawa. That is what Quebec Tory members do in Ottawa. Thank you, Michael Wilson!

Madam Speaker, Dr. Guillermo Ungo, Leader of the National Democratic Revolutionary Party of El Salvador, died February 28 while recuperating from brain surgery in Mexico.
Dr. Ungo, lawyer and academic, spent the sixties helping to organize a democratic socialist movement in which he became a leader in 1968 and formed a coalition with other parliamentary parties for peace and democracy.
After many coalition leaders were massacred in 1980, he travelled the world raising international support for peace and democracy in his homeland. In 1978 he was elected a vice-president of the Socialist International.
In 1988 he returned to El Salvador as presidential candidate of the Democratic Convergence in the March 1989 elections.
Since then, he campaigned for freedom of speech for churches, unions and other community groups in a national dialogue for peace. His party is contesting the mid-term elections in El Salvador on March 10,1991. He is remembered for his motto "It is not possible to be a democrat without being a revolutionary, nor to be a revolutionary without being a democrat".

subtopic: RESTORATION OF PEACE IN PERSIAN GULF
RESTORATION OF PEACE IN PERSIAN GULF
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, two days ago President Bush announced that operations in the Persian Gulf had been suspended, a moment we were all looking forward to. We can now expect peace to be restored in that part of the world, and we can only hope it will be a lasting peace. We must never forget that during these recent events, peace was always the primary motive in decisions made by this government. Our basic objective was to restore and maintain peace. I think this

reflects honourably on all Canadians. We shall continue to sursue that goal.

Madam Speaker, two weeks ago, the Northern Ontario Liberal caucus held meetings to hear presentations on the economy of the region. No one was surprised as each of the 57 witnesses confirmed this government's dismal handling of the economy. The government has created a "made-in-Canada" recession with its high interest rate policy.
The softwood lumber industry has crumbled. Exports to the U.S. are practically nil. The flow-through shares program was cancelled last year. Mineral exploration is down to 15 per cent from what it was five years ago.
In addition, the budget has cut $100 million from the job-training program. This will affect our youth and our laid-off workers.
Furthermore, the high cost of living that has resulted from the GST means that northern residents will not have that extra cash to invest in their RRSPs anymore.
This budget should have been introduced five years ago when the economy was strong. No, this government has chosen to hurt needy people while leaving their corporate friends unscathed.

Madam Speaker, this Conservative budget actually threatens to legislate contracting out.
What does this mean? It means that qualified government employees will see their jobs being given to this government's friends. It will become the worst institutionalized abuse of patronage, kickbacks and money laundering in history. These consultants, who often have no expertise and no experience, will receive their rewards through untendered contracts.
Tory bagmen, candidates, election organizers and contributors will charge the government hundreds of dollars
per day for work that could have been done by qualified regular government employees for a mere fraction of that rate.
In the last seven years, Conservatives have hired thousands of their friends through contracting out.
The Liberals were no better. One untendered contract was given in Manitoba to not one, not two but to three Liberal candidates, one of whom is now a member of this House.
Before the government is allowed to institutionalize and expand upon through legislation the abuses of themselves and the Liberals we need a truly independent report of the experiences of the last decade. Who received contracts?

Madam Speaker, the cynical measures in this government's budget to put a 3 per cent cap on all Public Service wage settlements and to threaten workers with job losses if they complain about it is nothing more than a mean-spirited, vicious assault on all Canadian workers.
By its own actions, this government is telling every employer in Canada that it is acceptable to throw away the right to bargain and it is acceptable to hold over the heads of workers the threats of job losses and contracting out.
If this government can be so cavalier at throwing away such basic, hard-won rights and principles of this nation's workers, will pay equity and equal opportunity be the next to go?
Who will be affected the most by this government's actions? The very members of our work force who are the most vulnerable: women, the disabled and visible minorities. Already their quality of life has been severely eroded by so many of this government's policies and now they are again in the direct line of fire.
This is clearly unacceptable and we, on this side of the House, will not stand for it.

Madam Speaker, I want to congratulate the federal government on its announcement last Tbesday night to move the
National Energy Board to Calgary. This is a positive step. It contributes to the goal of effective and efficient government decentralization and it recognizes the source of funds used to finance the National Energy Board's operations.
Some 14 to 15 months ago, I tabled a motion urging this government to make the move and we can now see it is a reality. Calgary is the energy capital of Canada and that is where the Board should be.

How come in 1980, 1981, 1982 it was propaganda, at least according to the Tories, and today, it is information? However, although I have no reservation about spending cuts in general, I must say I do not agree with the excessively high tax increases on tobacco products as proposed in this Budget. Madam Speaker, in my riding of Parkdale-High Park, there are more and more people out of work, both from plant closings and layoffs in the wake of the free trade agreement and the effects of the recession.
My constituents remember hearing the promise of retraining for workers who lose their jobs as a result of the free trade agreement. However, when they go to request that retraining, they are put on a waiting list and told it will be a year or more before they can get any training. Madam Speaker, they are out of work right now. They need to upgrade their skills right now if they are to move from jobs in light manufacturing and industry into the age of computers and technology. They are being left behind because the funds promised by this government are not available. Empty promises do not pay mortgages or feed families of Canadians. Empty promises do not prepare people for career changes in this age of technology. It is time to stop cutting training funds and start honouring the promise of retraining so that Canadians can work their way out of this recession and into the 21st century.

Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
Given his heartless budget this week, what does the minister have to say to the woman who is lined up today at the welfare office because she has no hope? What does he have to say to the child who this very noon will be eating lunch in a soup kitchen? What does the minister have to say to the grandmother whose operation is on hold because the hospital is too crowded? What does he have to say to the young person who will be sleeping in the street tonight because there is no more room at emergency shelters? What do the minister and the Prime Minister have to say to all those Canadians other than "Sorry, we have to fight the recession on your back"?
March 1, 1991

Madam Speaker, I do not think there is anybody in this House who is at all comfortable or happy to hear of the people who are at food banks or who are homeless, who are unemployed, who have lost their jobs or lost their homes. These are things that none of us like to contemplate at all and we are trying to do everything we can to deal with the difficulties that these people have in a variety of programs that are delivered at the federal, the provincial, and in many cases the municipal levels.
I think that my colleague, when she asks a question, is trying to deflect totally the concern of Canadians from the very, very real problem that we have of the debt in this country, and that each one of those Canadians whom my hon. friend refers to has indirectly, through the federal government, a debt of $15,000 that if we do not get under control, we are going to be able to help much less than we can now, because as that debt has mounted over the years, so has the cost of servicing that debt to the point now that 35 cents out of every revenue dollar goes simply to pay the interest on that debt. Those revenues cannot be used to help the homeless, to help the people who are unemployed or to help the people who are losing their jobs or a business.
You are making it worse.

My hon. friend says I am making it worse. Where he is quite wrong is that what this budget is precisely designed to do is to get interest rates down to ensure that we get a healthy economy to put those people back to work and to help the businesses create the jobs and the opportunities that will get them back to work.

Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance referred to the real problem. The real problem is that 200,000 children have to go to food banks to get something to eat. The real problem is that 1.5 million Canadians will not be able to find jobs when the government cuts its job-creation programs. The real problem is that tens of thousands of Canadians have no decent accommodation, and the government has decided to cut funding for subsidized housing. The real problem is that we are facing a crisis in our universal health care system, and the government goes and cuts $1 billion in this area.
Oral Questions
Does the minister realize that by abdicating his responsibility for dealing with the problems the provinces are facing, he is playing right into the hands of people who want to destroy our country? When will he understand the real problem?

Madam Speaker, I am sure the hon. member would be reluctant to say something she knows is wrong. During Question Period yesterday, in the House of Commons, I explained why the hon. member's statement is wrong.
My hon. friend referred to Tuesday's Budget. I would like to quote from page 89 of the English version, under the heading Cash and tax transfers to other levels of government. These transfers will increase from last year's $36.3 billion to $36.9 billion this year.
So my hon. friend knows perfectly well she is wrong, and the result is to mislead the Canadian people.
She knows that she has a responsibility as acting leader of her party to speak responsibly and honestly to Canadians.

Madam Speaker, the figures speak for themselves. The minister's own estimates tabled yesterday show a cut of more than $1 billion in federal payments for universal health care.
This budget is a separatist's dream. It is a federalist's nightmare.
At a time in the history of our country when the role of the federal government is under attack, the Conservatives are feeding the argument of those who want to tear this country apart. The Tories are doing the job by dismantling our national programs, bit by bit by bit.
Does the minister not understand that Canadians expect a national government to take care of the sick, the homeless and the jobless? Does the minister not understand that while John A. Macdonald was the Father of Confederation, his own Prime Minister has become the father of de-Confederation?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member asks to be taken seriously by Canadians when she demonstrates that she cannot even read the estimates. Transfers to the

provinces for health care this year will increase by about 1 per cent.
What the hon. member seeks to do is to confuse Canadians by completely ignoring the fact that transfers of tax points at exactly the same cost to the federal government as cash and at exactly the same benefit to the provinces as cash are increasing. She seeks deliberately to ignore that fact.
She talks about the effect on national unity. Yesterday she cited approvingly the comments that were made by her former chief organizer in Quebec, Mr. Cote. As she well knows, Mr. Cote advocates the dismantling of medicare and the destruction of our national health care system. Is that the policy of the national Liberal Party?

Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
When it signed its recent agreement on immigration with the Province of Quebec, the government said that from now on, constitutional negotiations would be approached as a single unit. In Tuesday's Budget, the government abandoned social policy to the provinces. It started its constitutional negotiations without public consultation. It ignored the advice of its experts.
My question is this: Why? Why do this with a single stroke of the arbitrary pen of the Minister of Finance?

Madam Speaker, I have had consultations with the provincial finance ministers on an ongoing basis. I indicated to them in both December and January the very serious nature of the fiscal problems of the federal government, and I gave them every indication that there would have to be changes to the transfers to the provinces in this budget. They understand that. They got that message very clearly back in the meeting in January.
My response to the hon. member is that we have had these discussions. We are going to have ongoing discussions with the provinces on the major transfers. We have discussions under way now and have had for about a year now on the changes to the equalization program.
We have also indicated to them our intention of bringing forward specific proposals on changes to the tax arrangements between the federal and provincial levels of government. There has been very, very extensive consultation.

Madam Speaker, this is not simply a financial debate; it is a constitutional debate. It is the same taxpayer. You have not changed the national deficit. You have simply transferred it from one level of government to another, and you have not done a thing.
What this government has done is that it has made exactly the same mistake in the constitutional debate that it made in the free trade agreement. There, desperate for a deal, the government made all kinds of concessions before the real negotiations even started. As a result, this government went to the negotiations with the Americans without any clothes on and got skinned.
Now, here, in the opening shots of the constitutional negotiations, the government has made the same cowardly mistake. It has given up all of the bargaining chips and, in doing so, has fundamentally altered the nature of the country.
My question is: How could this government play so fast and loose with the country? How could it so prejudice the nation without any kind of national consultation, without even the slightest hint of a national debate?

Madam Speaker, I think my hon. friend has this all wrong. He has to realize that what we are doing in the discussions that we are having with the provinces is not deciding on what powers the provinces should have or what powers the federal government should have. We are addressing a serious fiscal problem which I think, if he had the honesty to address himself, he would agree with me that we do have a serious fiscal problem and must deal with it.
He is saying we have a fiscal problem because of it. If he would be honest with himself and if he would be honest with the Canadian people, he would realize that in the 10 years leading up to 1984, when this government came into office, program spending increased by 13.8 per cent per annum. Since then it is 3.7 per cent per annum. The momentum that was created by that runaway spending of 13.8 per cent per annum created the problems that we are having to deal with today. That runaway spending at that time is taking away the choices that we have today
March 1, 1991

as a government, as Canadian people, and if we do not get the-
Order, order.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Increasingly, as people have had a chance to analyse this budget, they see that it is a budget designed to increase the recession, to deepen the recession, rather than to get people working, to get the poor back to earning a decent standard of living. This budget is clearly on the backs of the poor, the unemployed, and those in our society who have not had a chance. This finance minister is not giving them a chance.
The minister has said that this is a budget about choices. While others have said this will clearly deepen the recession, the choices the minister has chosen to make is to increase funding for Canada's spy agency by $24 million, to increase funding for the Senate by over $5 million, and to increase defence spending by almost a billion dollars. And yet he chose to cut jobs, cut medicare, cut social programs.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance: Will he stop cutting away at the things that help people in this country? Will he do something real for national unity and get Canadians back to work?

Madam Speaker, the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party referred to three programs. One of them increased, I think she said, by $20 million, the other by $5 million, and she knows that changing the funding in those programs would have had essentially no impact on the $35 billion deficit that we are looking at.
On the question of funding for defence, yes, we did have a choice.
Our choice was to assist and participate in the fight for freedom. If the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party is against fighting for freedom then she is in a different camp than we are on this side of the House, and let her stay in that camp because it is a camp that we do not want to be in.

Hear, hear.
Oral Questions

We did have choices. It is three days since the budget, and what I have heard from the New Democratic Party is that the New Democratic Party wants to spend additional amounts of money. As I said to her yesterday, when we open the books on the budget planning for 1991-1992 we are faced with a deficit of $35 billion. What I am hearing from her is that she would be quite comfortable to see that go up to $36 billion, $37 billion, or $38 billion.
Time and again she sat in this House and said: "Get interest rates down". Would she explain to me how moving the deficit from $35 billion up to $37 billion or $38 billion would get interest rates down? Or, would she admit, as I think she should know, that that would cause an increase in interest rates?

Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
There are people who say that there are a lot of dream projections in this budget. The minister is saying that the New Democratic Party has said we want to increase the deficit, that is absolutely wrong.
We are talking about priorities. He says $24 million for the spy agency, no money for the unemployed, and we say that is wrong.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the Minister of Finance. About a million and a half Canadians are now unemployed, and analysts say that the Budget will help push this figure even higher. The Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops commented that some thought should have been given to an approach that would have promoted job creation and a better distribution of wealth.
Why did the government decide against putting anything in the Budget to create jobs?

Madam Speaker, I believe that my hon. friend, Shirley Carr, the head of the Canadian Labour Congress, and the Catholic bishops have all said that we should get interest rates down.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party has said let us hope that interest rates come down. Hope will not bring interest rates down, but what will bring interest

March 1, 1991
Oral Questions
rates down are actions taken in this budget, which is precisely designed to bring interest rates down.
The limits on spending, the reductions in the deficit, and the inflation targets are all designed to bring down interest rates. If my hon. friend is looking for a way to help the unemployed, if she is looking for ways to help people get off the unemployed list, the best way that we can stimulate the economy is to bring down interest rates, and the fundamental design of this budget is to bring down interest rates, to stimulate the economy, and to generate employment.

Madam Speaker, day after day the minister stands in this House and says that he has to get inflation down to bring interest rates down. Maybe we do not disagree with that.
Then, why, I have to ask the minister, is he bringing in inflationary measures by introducing the GST that he knows caused the inflation rate to go up. He brings in a tax on cigarettes that he knows is inflationary. He increases unemployment insurance premiums that he knows is inflationary for small business and workers who have to pay that extra expense.
In addition and at the same time this finance minister says that he is not destroying the national medicare system. I want to say to him that we know he did not start that destruction-

speechtext: I am sure the hon. member will put her question.

Madam Speaker, I want to ask the minister who has said-and the minister of health-that the medicare system is not being destroyed and that the reduction in transfer payments started by the Liberals is not destroying medicare if they will not listen to their own National Council on Welfare that says this federal government's budget can mean the end of medicare. If they will not listen to the people of Canada, will they listen to their own advisory council?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I almost could not believe my own ears. Is the hon. member saying on behalf of her party that she opposes the measures taken by the Minister of Finance to reduce by 100,000 the number of teenage smokers in Canada? If that is her policy, let her say so explicitly.
I strongly support that policy, a policy that will save thousands of lives in this country, that will save tens of millions of dollars in our health care budgets. If the NDP believes that taxes should not be increased to discourage young smokers, let it say so.
In so far as the National Council on Welfare is concerned, its responsibility is to argue for more spending on behalf of social programs, and it does that job well.
In this House of Commons, the responsibility of the hon. member and of members on this side is not only to say where we would favour more spending but also where we would get the money from. It is time to come clean with Canadians and for the Leader of the NDP to spell it out.

Madam Speaker, my question for to the Minister of Finance.
Regrettably, yesterday the Prime Minister was unable to answer questions regarding allegations that have been made by Mr. Robert Normand, a member of the Spicer Commission.
Given that the Prime Minister and the government have both a moral and legal obligation for the proper operation of the commission, will the Minister of Finance tell the House of Commons today, and through the House the people of Canada, whether or not there is any substance to Mr. Normand's allegation that some commission members may be collecting up to $18,000 a month, improperly?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think it is veiy important to reiterate that Mr. Normand at no time has suggested that anyone is doing anything fraudulent on the commission. He stated that quite unequivocally.
The hon. member knows very well, as we stated in the House yesterday, that a commission such as the Spicer commission operates independently.
Although it was announced at the beginning of November, the financial requirements for 1991-92 are still under consideration and will be included in the Supplementary Estimates for 1991-92. The financial requirements for this year, 1990-91, will be part of the final
March 1, 1991
