Supplementary Estimates that will be tabled in Parliament shortly, so there will be an opportunity for parliamentary overview.
But I would remind the hon. member that although the commission is independent, it does come under the purview of the Auditor General.

Madam Speaker, the commission was appointed by the Prime Minister and cabinet to do important work; that is, to deal with the question of national unity. This is an important question for Canada. It cannot operate under a cloud raised by an eminent member of the commission, not by the opposition, not by outside parties.
I again ask the Minister of Justice whether or not she understands the importance of clearing the air of this dark cloud that has been raised and put above the commission by a member of the commission. Will she make a full report to Parliament and to Canadians that indeed no member of this commission is being paid $18,000 a month, supposedly picking the brains of Canadians to solve the problem of national unity?
Canadians want to know that these commissioners are doing their job: picking our brains, not picking our pockets.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, once again I repeat: the hon. member knows that this is an independent commission. I am sure that if I or any of my colleagues sought to interfere in its activities, the hon. member would be the first on his feet in this House to complain.
I think that if the hon. member wishes to contribute to the clarity of the process and the ability of the commission to make a contribution, he will avoid making statements that put the commission under a cloud. Although the commission is independent, it does not operate at large; it does not operate without any constraints.
We have a process of auditing all of the commissions of Parliament precisely to avoid the kind of thing that the hon. member is talking about. Those proper agencies will do their job to assure the Canadian people that then-money is being properly spent, and that is how it ought to be.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for Canada Post. As of today postal rates for many weekly newspapers will jump dramatically, some over 1,000 per cent. The minister has made the situation even worse by giving half the papers a three-month reprieve yesterday while throwing the rest to the wolves today. This will wipe out many valuable weekly farming community publications right across this country.
Will the minister assure us in this House today that these ludicrous rate increases will be stopped in their tracks?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
What is ludicrous are the comments made by the hon. member about what is happening.
As was announced some two years ago, the subsidies for publications are being reduced as part of the fiscal management of the government. What was announced yesterday were the rates which will apply for weekly newspapers. There is a 90-day delay for the small town weekly newspapers in terms of its implementation.
There was also, at the same time, an announcement that there would be an additional $2 million of subsidy available for these broader regional weeklies to which I think the hon. member was referring.
The matter is being dealt with sensitively, properly and in an expeditious manner, as is usually the case with this government.

Madam Speaker, half of them are being driven out on the street today. The minister has not addressed the problem.
Does the minister not realize that these weeklies operate on a paper-thin profit margin and any increase in postal rates would close many of them down? The minister has attacked rural post offices and he is now laying siege to rural communication lines. Will the minister tell Canada Post that it can no longer add to its fat profits on the backs of rural Canadians?

Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member's use of hyperbole is quite astounding. He is following the example of the deputy leader of his party, I guess.
The continuous program, administered by the Department of Communications for quite a number of years, long before this government came into office, is a program of subsidy to publications in this country. Weekly newspapers, small town newspapers for towns under 10,000 population will continue to have the first 2,500 copies delivered by Canada Post free of charge.
As a result of the adjustments, on average across the country, these small town weekly newspapers will pay in the order of eight or nine cents a copy for delivery. When you compare that to the 40 cents which it costs to deliver a first class letter or a smaller package, I think he will realize that in fact the program is still quite generous, in recognition of the important role of the small town newspapers.
What is needed is understanding by everybody involved. It is not aided by the wild hyperbole, exaggeration and mistruths of the hon. member.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance, who continues today to talk about the serious fiscal problems facing the Government of Canada and the need for everybody to contribute.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance why he has not changed the interest deductibility rule. Is he aware that at a recent tax conference in New Zealand, a New Zealand multinational by the name of Fletcher Challenge bragged about setting up in Canada, because Canada was a tax haven, which enabled it to make $128 million in 1989 and pay absolutely no taxes at all, because Canada is a place where it can borrow money to finance its global operations and at the same time avoid taxes. If the Minister of Finance is interested in reducing the deficit, why did he not do something about that and why did he extend that rule in December 1990, rather than getting rid of it?

Madam Speaker, on the question of interest deductibility, interest is deductible if it is used in borrowing money, if it is paid on borrowed money designed to earn profits for the company that is incurring that deduction. The Fletcher people are taking advantage of a particular tax provision, which is available in many other countries of the world today. It is designed to generate profits here in Canada. Those profits will be fully taxable.

Madam Speaker, the fact is that it helps them to generate profits all over the world which are not generated in Canada. The only people who are affected are the Canadian taxpayers who end up financing Fletcher Challenge to the tune of millions of dollars.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance, who talks so soberly about sharing the burden, why he refuses to do anything about that kind of rule. Why does he allow the Canadian taxpayers to continue to be pillaged by these multinational corporations. Why, for instance, he is not willing to do anything about the business and entertainment tax loophole, the free lunch loophole which is worth $1 billion in free lunches to the business community-
Why did he not have the nerve to ask them to contribute to reducing the deficit? Why do they continue to get a free lunch?

Madam Speaker, we did change the business entertainment expense. We brought it into line with what the provision is in other countries, in particular in the United States. My hon. friend can rail away as much as he wants about the provisions in the corporate income tax system.
If he would study the corporate income tax system, he would realize that it is just on the margin of competitiveness in relation to our major trading partner, the United States.
We could raise our taxes. We could eliminate a number of the provisions in the corporate income tax system, but the result would be that companies like Flyer Industries in his riding would move down to Minneapolis. He might feel very good about the change in the income tax system, but he would be the first up on his hind legs in this House saying: "Why are you doing things that are causing companies to leave Canada and move to the United States?"
March 1, 1991

That is precisely why we have to maintain a corporate income tax system that is competitive in this country.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Last year in passing Bill C-21, the government made a legislative commitment to freeze unemployment insurance premiums for three years. In announcing this freeze, the minister said: "The government will continue to finance any deficits in the unemployment insurance account in difficult times when it may not be appropriate to allow premiums to rise."
That is what the minister said. Why then is the minister now increasing unemployment insurance premiums by $2 billion when we are in a serious recession? He himself says that we are in difficult times. Why is he breaking his word of last year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member well knows that under the Unemployment Insurance Act there is a requirement that premiums be established to keep returning the fund to a balanced position.
In other words, if there is a deficit, there is a requirement in the law that premiums increase, and, if there is a surplus, that they go down. When the premiums were established in the last budget, it was done in the expectation and the forecast of what the economy would look like at the time.
Those circumstances have changed. The government will continue to fund the deficit throughout the period. The fund will be in deficit and the government will cany it. In order to bring it back to balance, otherwise premiums will have to increase faster. If we did not increase premiums now, they would have to go to $4 or $5 at the end of the period to cover that deficit.

Madam Speaker, the fact is that in 1990 the Minister of Finance made a commitment to freeze unemployment insurance premiums for three years.
Oral Questions
The minister said in his budget that in hard times, he would cover deficits out of general revenue. That is what he said, and now he is making a $2 billion flip-flop.
Let me have this answer, Madam Speaker. Was the minister totally incompetent when he made that legislative commitment last year, or was he simply lying to the Canadian people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly think that the question is an offensive one.
It is certainly offensive because we are continuing to carry the fund while it is in deficit. I would remind the hon. member that it was his party which delayed this whole project well beyond where it might have been providing some better use during the recession.
He also knows that we are going to continue to carry the fund while it is in deficit.

Madam Speaker, Canada's cultural community is already singing the "Bye Bye Blues" with the Wilson budget cuts and delays of $197 million.
Will the Minister of Communications walk over to his friend, the Minister of Finance, as he carves up grants and contributions, and tell him that at a time of strained national unity, this government should be strengthening the ties that bind us rather than following a search and destroy mission against Canadian culture.

Madam Speaker, the government is very much aware of the importance of cultural activities in Canada, and that is why it has made available to government agencies and the Department of Communications the kind of funding we need-which compares favourably with other activity sectors-to define policy and be present in all cultural areas in this country.

March 1, 1991
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, it is a sad day when the Minister of Communications becomes the minister of vacation and is not around to defend Canada's cultural community.
In the same vein, funding to women's research groups has not been restored and small group funding has sustained a $75 million cut this year alone.
Will the Minister of Finance admit that research and community development is at least half of the equality battle-if he cares-and refuse to strangle these groups and their work for women any longer?

Madam Speaker, the government has added $8 million this year to the Canada Council, for the arts.
Furthermore, the government is also actively involved in our cultural industries because the market situation in Canada is a difficult one. In addition to investing in these agencies, the govemement must also ensure that our cultural industries develop as they should, in order to support our cultural market. It is with this in mind, Madam Speaker, that the government has tried to provide for a fair distribution of programs and grants between these agencies and the Department of Communications.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. He has just responded to my colleague from Winnipeg by suggesting that we have to keep our tax system in this country somehow competitive with other countries and that justifies the very gross loopholes which exist in our tax system.
Let me ask the Minister of Finance this. The United States, which is our major trading partner, has a minimum corporate tax. It has just put into effect a luxury tax. It has an inheritance tax. All of these are things which we do not have in this country. Let me ask this minister why he is not prepared to put these kinds of fair
measures into the tax system to help Canadians and to give the ordinary person a tax break?

Madam Speaker, I want to ask my hon. friend whether the United States has a large corporations tax. I want to ask my friend whether the United States has as high a capital gains tax rate in that country as we do? We have a higher burden on corporations than the United States. What one has to look at is the bottom line on the corporate tax system.
As I said to his colleague from Winnipeg, we can have a good time feeling warm all over by hammering the corporations and raising the tax rates, but the people who live in his community would find that the jobs would not be there. They would have to go across the border to Detroit and get jobs in Detroit because the businesses would not be able to support the same type of activity in Windsor as they could working across the way in Detroit.
His community is fortunate because people can go across the river, but people who live in other communities are not be so fortunate. It is for that reason we must have a corporate income tax system which is not just somehow competitive but actually competitive, to ensure that we retain jobs here in Canada and not export them to the United States.

Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance cannot have it both ways. He cannot say we have to be competitive and so we have to keep our tax system in line with other countries and, when we point out to him the tax system in the United States has these various mechanisms which in fact hit higher income people and large corporations, he says: "Oh well, we cannot do that".
Why is the Minister of Finance prepared to use the excuse of the United States when it is to his benefit? Why is he not prepared to use the example of the United States to put fairness into our tax system as it should be?

Madam Speaker, the only point that I was making is that the United States has a very complex corporate minimum tax and, rather than have that corporate minimum tax which adds a lot of complexity to the tax system, we have the large corporations tax which is very simple and has the same sort of impact. That was the only point that I was making.
March 1, 1991

Now the hon. member refers to fairness in taxation on individuals. If he would refer to a study that has been recently completed by the Organization of Economic Co-operation, the OECD in Paris, it shows that the Canadian tax system for the average worker is a fair tax system, that the take home pay after taxes for Canadian workers is on the high end of the range.
He will also be aware, I am sure, of a study that was done by Price Waterhouse comparing the tax system for upper income people in Canada and the United States. It indicates that the tax burden on upper income people in Canada is considerably greater than the tax system in the United States.

My question is directed to the Minister of Forestry. For many months, the Canadian government has tried to conclude a Canada-Quebec agreement on the forestry sector, and we all know that the federal Department of Forestry is prepared to inject $100 million to help forestry workers in Quebec this year. The question is this: Could the minister inform the House today whether he is pursuing his talks with Quebec for the purpose of concluding an agreement on the Quebec forestry sector, because forestry workers in Abitibi-Temiscamingue are sick and tired of waiting for the province to make up its mind?

Madam Speaker, my discussions with my counterpart in the province of Quebec are ongoing. They are progressing toward a new agreement that would respect both the objectives of the province of Quebec as well as certain legitimate national objectives.
Keeping in mind that the provinces, of course, own and have the principal responsibility for the management of the resource, we have a number of serious national objectives which we are attempting to pursue. A few of those are the stabilization of private woodlots in the provinces, research, environmental questions and general labour and manpower questions.
I made an offer to the province of Quebec on August 24 and I am hoping to have an agreement completed within the not too distant future.
Oral Questions PUBLIC SERVICE

Madam Speaker, at a time when the unemployment rate and the welfare rolls are skyrocketing, the Minister of Finance, who has predicted a 10 per cent unemployment rate, has now frozen public servant wages, including those of the armed services whom the government has just congratulated for a job well done.
This government has declared open season on public servants across Canada, be they federal, provincial, municipal or school board employees. All public servants will be affected by this Tory budget. How can the Minister of Finance stand in this House and say that by gouging one group, the public servants of Canada, he is correcting the economic difficulties caused by his own incompetence.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Does Sheila write everybody's question?

In this budget we are not attempting to gouge anybody. What we are putting forward in a very clear way is an assessment of the problems of this country. We have a serious fiscal problem. We are asking the employees as well as members of Parliament and ministers to participate in the solution of this major fiscal problem. We have asked the public servants to be a part of that and recognize that their position in the country as a group which provides some leadership, some direction for the over all country can help in getting the costs of the Public Service down.
What I hear time and again from private sector people is the costs of government are getting too high. Provincial governments and municipal governments have been entering into wage settlements in the past couple of years two and three percentage points higher than the rate of inflation. If what we do in Ottawa can help them bring their level of increase down to a level that is more consistent with what the private sector can afford, then the economy of this country is going to be better off for it. We will become more competitive. There will be more job opportunities or more business opportunities, and that is going to be a very important element in getting the economy going again and creating the revenues that pay our public servants.

Tributes

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is my unhappy duty to advise the House that we will be hearing tributes to a former colleague.
I will call first on the hon. member for Calgary Southwest.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to pay a very special tribute to a long time friend, a colleague of this House who passed away last evening, Peter C. Bawden.
Peter was bom and raised in Toronto and moved to Alberta in the very early 1950s where he pioneered the oil well drilling business. Bawden Drilling was formed about 1952, and as the company grew and expanded and became more specialized, its drilling rigs could be found operating in Alberta, British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Sable Island, the far northern Arctic, Winter Harbour on Melville Island, the United States, California, Central and South America, Australia, Indonesia, Iran, and the North Sea, all operating with onshore and offshore facilities.
Safety was always one of Peter's goals; to make sure the men who operated the equipment were well informed, well protected and well trained. He started in the very beginning always having a drilling safety supervisor who worked the rigs, ensuring that peoples lives came first.
He loved sports. He was involved in the aviation industry. Peter was everywhere. He served on many boards, various charities and at the University of Calgary. He gave so much of his life to his community of Calgary, to the province of Alberta and, indeed, to all of Canada.
Peter Bawden served in this House as a Conservative member of Parliament from 1972 to 1979, working in so many ways, always for a better Canada. It was just over a year ago when Peter received the Order of Canada, recognizing his givings, his talents, his accomplishments and his contributions.
All of us here today regret the loss of a dear colleague and extend our very deepest sympathy to his wife Margaret and to his children; Jennifer, David, John, Valerie, Kate and Louise.
I thank you, and God bless Peter.

Mr. Speaker, we are all very saddened to hear of the untimely passing of Peter Colwell Bawden, internationally known in the petroleum industry, a very highly successful businessman. Those of us who served with him saw how well he represented his constituents.
I was surprised when he decided to retire in 1979, having been elected in 1972 and successfully re-elected in 1974. I had the privilege of knowing him very well. I repeat again, we were all very surprised when he decided not to run in 1979. May I say we were all disappointed when he announced his decision that he would rather concentrate all his activity on his highly well known business enterprise where he was so successful.
What we remember of him is that he always conducted himself as a perfect gentleman, a very highly sensitive person. These are times to reflect on these great qualities that Peter Colwell Bawden represented so well.
Our leader has asked me, on behalf of our party, to extend our very sincere sympathy to his wife, whom some of us knew very well, and to his children.

Mr. Speaker, it is a real shock to hear of the passing of Peter Bawden. I knew Peter very, very well. Peter was one of those members of Parliament who was well liked on all sides of the House, who was well known on all sides of the House.
One of the things that struck me about Peter was that after he left this place, he still kept in touch with a number of us who were his friends during the days that he was a member of Parliament representing the city of Calgary.
Peter brought to the House of Commons expert knowledge in the field of energy, in the field of business and a real concern for his community of Calgary, a concern about sports and a concern about education. He was recognized by his country, as my friend from Calgary has just said, when he received the Order of Canada just a short while ago.
He will be missed by all of us. On behalf of my party and myself, I want to extend our sincere condolences to his wife, to his family and to his many, many friends not just in the city of Calgary, but indeed right across this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):

Mr. Speaker, I just want to add on behalf of the government a couple of words about Peter Bawden who, as the member for Yorkton-Melville has just commented, even though he left this House in 1979 to devote full time to his business, did keep in touch. I can say personally, as a good, close friend of Peter and Margaret, that of all the friends and associates he had around the world-and he had them around the world because of his business interests-and across the country, none he valued more than the associations he made here in this House. It was for that reason he kept in such close touch.
It is tragic that he died at this very early age. My wife and I had the pleasure of spending a couple of days with Peter and Margaret just after the new year. Even then, in the late stages of his illness he had that tremendous interest in what was going on, constantly probing, asking and suggesting. It was part of his character to be terrifically interested in what was happening to this country, what was happening on the political scene, to be vitally concerned about it and doing what he could right up to the very end to try to make things better. We will all miss him.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):

Mr. Speaker, just a word or two for those of us who are involved in the energy portfolio. Peter Bawden not only was a pioneer in that industry, but remained an adviser to me almost to the end.
Peter had a very great sense of life. I remember not only being elected in 1972 with Peter, but in 1973 the government convened the Western Economic Opportunities Conference in Calgary. Peter had just been newly elected and I remember our attendance at that conference. Peter saw us on one of the major access roads into Calgary. He stopped his vehicle, backed up the wrong way in traffic and invited us to the conference. That was Peter in a very direct and human way. While we were partisans here, he was a friend to all of us outside of the House.
Just a last point, Peter exemplified in the oil industry possibly the very pioneering spirit that has marked that industry. He came from a background that was not at all the derring-do of the industry and the men and women who were its pioneers. Peter exemplified that. When I became minister of energy, he only had words of support

speechtext: We are now starting the five-minute period of questions and comments following the speech by the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on questions and comments, the member who spoke on behalf of the New Democratic Party is the labour critic of our caucus.
I was spokesperson of our caucus when the Liberals introduced their legislation in the mid-1980s when they broke the collective agreements that the government itself had signed with the Public Service of Canada.
I know the hardship and the bad feelings that existed among the Public Service at that time, the time of the six and five legislation. I wonder how our critic views the threats that were in the throne speech where the government said, for example, that it was going to negotiate the right to contract out with the Public Service, but, in the very next sentence of the throne speech: "-and if we do not get our way we are going to legislate our way".
The whole idea of collective bargaining is that the two sides come together and try to resolve their differences. I wonder how our member feels about the threat that the government makes when the government says that it does not matter whether it negotiates or not because it is going to get its way through legislation. This is just like the Liberals who actually broke the collective agreements that they themselves had signed with the Public Service.
We now have a new government, the Conservative government, saying it will negotiate but if it does not get its way it is going to legislate. I wonder how the member feels about that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, one of the hon. members across the way said "disappointed". Outraged, I think, would be a more appropriate term.
This government has not just threatened the public sector with legislation, this government has guaranteed in its budget that it will legislate the public sector workers. In doing that, it has threatened private sector workers that they will be next. Because what will automatically happen is that pressure will be on to

March 1, 1991
The Budget
reduce and tighten the screws on workers in other sectors while profits continue not to be controlled.
We will then have our well-educated, dedicated, hard-working Canadian workers creating a Maquiladora north with the low wages and poverty, and the rich collecting large profits.
This is is not short-term. This is a long-term plan to ensure that Canadian workers and their families suffer under the kind of government this government is offering us.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the member for Mission-Coquitlam about her excellent comments about this government's budget and, in particular, the reference in her speech to the concerns across the country now, particularly in our home province of British Columbia, about transfer payments to the provinces.
The member will know well that when the Liberals were in office part of their six and five program was the lifting of the requirement that federal funds for post-secondary education and health were required to be spent in that area.
We have the premier of British Columbia, Mr. Vander Zalm, a former Liberal himself, and the Liberal Party now and we are not sure if that is still their position.
My question to the member is, what does she think about that proposal? Would she support a measure that would ensure that federal funds on health and education are, in fact, spent on health and education in the provinces?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague who asked the question.
One of the serious flaws in this government's policy of cutting back on transfer payments is that while the national standards that the government sets and this Parliament sets regarding how health care and education should be delivered in the provinces is already being eroded under this kind of budgetary plan. With fewer and fewer dollars going to the provinces, there will be less and less control on maintenance of national standards.
In my constituency of Mission-Coquitlam, nurses have been laid off just recently and health care workers in the hospital there cannot keep up with the numbers of
people who are seeking health care. Nurses are being laid off, and that was before the budget.
This government, if it indeed takes its responsibilities for health care and education seriously, has to maintain the position that it imposed and ensured that national standards are maintained. This government must, very much, rethink its policies.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am quite pleased to have an opportunity to join today in this budget debate. Before I get started, I would like to congratulate the Minister of Finance who has done a masterful job of steering the economy in the right direction despite the constraints he is faced with as a result of years of mismanagement by the previous administration-17 years at least.
I am not the only one who says this. The Hon. Frank McKenna, the premier of New Brunswick, pointed it out in a speech last week. He said: "The Liberal governments of the 1960s and the 1970s and up to 1984 had abandoned their principles by spending beyond their limits and creating a massive deficit, in effect a mortgage on the future of Canada".
The policies of the Liberals in the 1960s and 1970s undermined our long-term ability to be productive and in 1984 we decided to change the course.
In our first year of government, we established an agenda for economic renewal which outlined the competitive challenge which was faced by Canada. Subsequently we have worked to provide a better framework for restoring productivity growth.
I think it is fair to say that Canadians are increasingly concerned about our ability to compete. What we have tried to do in this budget is re-establish once again the foundation to enable us to compete through the 1990s.
We feel that governments have a responsibility to create an environment that encourages the growth of competitive enterprise. What we have done in the 1991 budget is set out a plan for economic recovery, actions which will restore our fiscal balance and move toward price stability.
There is a great deal more that has to be done to ensure our future prosperity, but if we can boost our productivity growth then our prosperity will be ensured for forthcoming generations.
March 1, 1991

This is not something that can be done just by governments. We need the assistance of the private sector. We have to create an atmosphere and opportunities for the private sector and we have to try to maximize our productivity growth.
We need to examine the quality of our investments in infrastructure, machinery, and equipment, training, education, research and development, and private sector spending on training and research. That is not just an issue for government. It is an issue for business and for labour as well.
All of us can help to strengthen our competitive ability by identifying problems and developing solutions. We intend as a government to launch a national effort to build a partnership for prosperity that draws fully on the talents and efforts of Canadians in every sector of economic life.
In my capacity as Minister of Transport, I would like to take a minute within the context of the budget debate to describe some of the initiatives which we are taking at Transport Canada to face the challenges of tomorrow.
We are working in partnership with the private sector, in communities across Canada, to try and find those solutions. First, in airport devolution. We have taken some firm steps toward the management of Canada's auports. Our policy on the transfer of airports to local airport authorities allows the communities to have a greater say in the business of their airports.
What we are trying to do through the creation of these local airport authorities is serve the interests of the communities, enhance regional economic development potential, and permit our national airport system to operate in a more cost-effective and commercial manner. It will create, we feel, a new spirit of competition among airports and thus the communities of Canada.
When I was in the United States a couple of weeks ago talking with some financial analysts, they told us that over the past ten years they have gotten away from the airport, non-aviation side, being run by engineers and accountants and more and more they are run by people with marketing experience. I think we are going to see in Canada, through the devolution of these airports, economic opportunities open up for us.
The Budget
We have reached an agreement in principle with the Edmonton Regional Airport Authority. We are negotiating with Vancouver, Calgary and Montreal and we expect that in the course of this year we will finalize those negotiations. As well, there are several other communities that have expressed interest in this type of airport operation.
This, I would suggest, is an indication of the government's commitment to provide for sound and representative economic management, as well as ensure competitiveness in the transportation system.
When I got this job the Prime Minister said to me: "Lewis, I want you to fix Pearson". I set about trying to continue the work done by previous Ministers of Transport to expand this wonderful facility as much as possible. As everybody knows, Pearson is the cornerstone of our aviation system and as a result of years of neglect, the infrastructure at Lester B. Pearson International Airport is showing. We have made a commitment to fix Pearson and to make it a world class facility. As the House knows, it is the hub of Canada's aviation system, the third largest gateway to North America. It is big business.
It is big business in this way: I do not think Canadians realize what an economic engine Pearson and other airports can be. Pearson directly and indirectly employs
60,000	people; 14,000 people go to work at Pearson every day. It brings in $630 million in taxes to three levels of government and $4 billion in business revenue. The economic impact of Pearson and other airports across the country is tremendous.
But at Pearson we had a difficulty. We had a facility built for eight million passengers a year accommodating 21 million passengers a year. We went to the private sector with Terminal 3. We opened it last week, increasing our capacity by 40 per cent. We feel this is a milestone in Canada's aviation system, because it was built at no cost to the taxpayer. It is owned by the private sector. It is proof that we can have a partnership between government and the private sector that can bring benefits to the country.
I would suggest that Canadians are going to be boasting about Pearson International Airport around the world and visitors from around the world are going to be envious.

March 1, 1991
The Budget
At the same time, we are improving Terminals 1 and 2. A $40 million extension to the international wing of Terminal 2 was opened in December; which provides new gates for wide-body aircraft. We have increased the customs capacity at the terminal. We opened the first phase of a $52 million package of improvements to Terminal 2's domestic wing in January. The second phase we expect will be finished later this year. We have opened it up with windows, skylights and moving sidewalks, and have improved the baggage handling facility.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: State of the art.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think it is. It is state of the art now and we have more improvements we want to make.
As well, we have announced that we intend to go to the private sector to participate in the further modernization of the two terminals.
We have an Environmental Assessment Review Panel under way to see what new runway capacity we can add to Pearson. That work is well under way and we expect the results of that sometime later this year.
People might ask, why am I emphasizing Pearson? I am emphasizing it because 60 per cent of our aviation traffic travels through Pearson one way or another, is affected by Pearson in any one day. Modem facilities at Pearson are essential to the economic and social development of metro Toronto, the surrounding communities in southern Ontario and, in fact, all of Canada.
On the international scene, we are working to improve an air agreement with the United States that, quite frankly, is archaic and restrictive. We want an air agreement that will bring to Canadians the benefits of a competitive air transportation network that is responsive to market demands and new opportunities. We want an agreement that will enable our business people to do business in the United States. We want an agreement that is going to get Canadians out of the airport lounges and into their customers' boardrooms to sell the products and the services which Canadians provide so well.
When I became Minister of Transport, as I travelled around this country, community after community-Halifax, Kelowna, Moncton, Calgary, Montreal, Thunder Bay-all said: "Look, we need a new agreement", and they know that if we are going to put this recession
behind us, we have to get into the United States to sell our products.
We realize that these are difficult times for Canadian airlines, but that is no different than anywhere else in the world. Carriers all around the world are encountering difficulties. But we have confidence in the Canadian airline industry and are confident that, given the right environment, given a level playing field, Canadians can compete with anybody. We are looking for an agreement that responds to market forces and demands which allow the carriers of both countries to take advantage of new market opportunities and a regime that is as expansive as possible.
We want better services for the communities of Canada, better services for the consumers of Canada and better opportunities for Canadian airlines. We are under way on that and I am quite optimistic that we can negotiate a better deal, a better deal for our Canadian carriers, consumers and communities.
I should not spend all my time on the aviation side of things. I have come to realize, although it might be said I am an individual with not much maritime exposure, the importance of shipping to all Canadians. I thought I might get some applause from that. That is a bit of a conflict of interest there.
But I realize that the financial stability of the marine industry is important to us. I realize that marine issues are just as important if you are trying to ship grain out of Saskatchewan as if you are in one of the ports. We are spending time on that because our ships move wheat from Saskatchewan. They move iron ore from Quebec, potash from Saskatchewan, steel from Ontario and petrochemicals from Alberta, and so we have paid some attention to marine policy.
There are two things I would like to talk about today, one of which is our efforts to try to achieve greater delegation of authority for the port system of Canada. Ports Canada, as the House will know, administers the major commercial ports and some local port corporations. This is a Crown corporation which has been quite profitable over the past four years and it has returned some $250 million worth of dividends to the Government of Canada.
We want to enable the ports to mature and be competitive. We are going to delegate it more authority
March 1, 1991

so that they have the opportunity to expand their operations and be competitive within the marine system.
I also would point out that the government recently announced an initiative to make us better able to compete as a maritime nation.
We have the international maritime centres legislation, which will enable international shipping companies to locate in Canada. We think that this legislation, which was announced last week, will bring shipping executives, maritime law experts, marine architects and a host of other shipping professionals to Canada to develop an enhanced marine sector that we do not now have. As well, we are looking at our ability to get containers in and out of the ports more efficiently. I am expecting to receive a study on container competitiveness very soon so that we can see what we can do as a government to facilitate an improvement in that system.
Last summer I became involved in trying to sort out some difficulties in the trucking industry. I want to report to the House that we commissioned some studies through Transport Canada, because I was quite frankly fed up with having 14 different theories on what the tax system was in Canada and the United States, whether I got them from the trucking industry, from Finance, or wherever. We have formed a steering committee of all the stakeholders, and when we get these studies done, we will know exactly what the situation is and try to take some corrective measures.
One aspect of transport that was touched on, not so much in the budget, but as affecting transport was the legislation for disabled Canadians. I was quite pleased with the efforts of the finance minister to assist disabled Canadians. What I have tried to do is to put a focus on the disabled in transport. The House will know that the disability tax credit is going to be increased from $575 to $700 as of the 1991 taxation year. Perhaps more important, the definition of expenses eligible for that tax credit is going to be broadened and will include the cost of part-time attendants in the home. Costs incurred by employers in modifying their premises to accommodate disabled persons will become fully deductible in the year in which they are incurred. Benefits provided by employers to disabled persons to enable or assist them to work will no longer be taxable.
The Budget
I dealt with this when I was Minister of Justice, and I am pleased to tell the House that, as Minister of Transport, we have carried the focus into transport. The House will know that the government provided some $3 million over the last five years to 130 communities across Canada for the Accessible Vehicle Acquisition Program.
We have an advisory committee on the disabled, which is comprised of some 17 representatives of consumer groups and six industry representatives. We have had some meetings and we have been able to achieve some improvements. Last fall I announced that there had been an agreement between the Air Transport Association of Canada and Transport Canada to provide Braille and large print safety cards on commercial airlines for a one-year demonstration period. If that is successful, it will be carried on.
I think we have been able to do some things in transport which co-ordinate with what the minister has done in his budget, and I can assure the House that we will continue to do so.
I want to touch on something in the budget as an employer.
The Minister of Transport has, under his jurisdiction in transport, some 20,000 public servants. I found in my travels that they work pretty hard for the government. Some of them, as the House knows, do not always have the safest jobs in the world; I am talking about search and rescue jobs. The public servants employed by the Ministry of Transport-and I think it is fair to say at all levels of the federal government, in all ministries-I have found by and large work very hard for the government. I appreciate that there is a 3 per cent cap on increases, and I appreciate that this is probably going to be difficult. But I think we all have to try to play a part in the difficulties that we are facing. I know that the public servants who are very loyal to the government and to the country understand what we are going through. I just wanted to recognize the contribution the public servants make in Transport Canada, especially, and in other areas. I am sure the measures that have to be taken will be taken with some sensitivity by all departments. Especially, we will try to do that in Transport.
In closing my remarks, I would say that we have demonstrated in this government leadership in terms of our financial difficulties. We have had to take some hard choices. It would be much more pleasant to be doing

The Budget
some nice things with money but we do not have it. We do not have the money to throw at problems. Canadians realize that running a government is just like running their daily lives. They are not stupid. We have a situation on our hands and they realize, just as though it were their household budget, that we have to get it under control. They are looking for fiscal responsibility and other responsibilities from government.
I say that we have given fiscal responsibility the people of Canada since 1984-that may be a measure of debate for my friends across the way-and we will continue to do that for the rest of our mandate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a couple of questions on two particular items for the minister. First of all, up front, I want to thank the minister for his co-operation on the development of Bathurst Municipal Airport. I know he has talked about Pearson airport and its importance to millions of travellers, but we have smaller airports in the country and I want to take the opportunity to thank him for his assistance with the Bathurst municipal airport. We know it is a complicated situation with airports of that size across the country.
I would ask him if he has any plans to get involved, because we have seen mention of user fees in the budget, in some sharing of administrative costs. He will be aware that we have been in touch on this matter. It is an unusual situation so I would like to have him comment on if he feels there is any way the government can participate in some of the operating costs of the smaller airports on a shared basis or whatever because there have been reports through the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans in New Brunswick that there may be some assistance forthcoming.
The only other point I would like to have the minister comment on, because I know a number of my colleagues want to chat with him also, is the Trans-Canada Highway in New Brunswick. As he will know, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Newfoundland are interested in the Trans-Canada Highway because there is so much land transport across that area now. The budget and the estimates did not have anything specific with respect to the Trans-Canada that I could find. So I wonder if he would comment on those two issues.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to thank my hon. friend for his comments. There has been a fair amount of activity in the smaller airports in New Brunswick. I think actually if I were to guess it would probably run Ontario, B.C., New Brunswick in terms of what we have been trying to do for smaller airports. I certainly am paying attention to my hon. friend's comments and to those of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans with respect to what we can do at Bathurst.
With respect to the Trans-Canada Highway this has been the subject of much discussion and much study. I would hope that this year we can take a look at our national roads policy and decide whether or not we should take a run at a comprehensive national roads policy which would involve some 23,000 or 24,000 kilometres of our national highway system in order to upgrade it. I especially appreciate the problems in New Brunswick. They are being attended to now I believe by the province and if there is a way we can become involved in that we will certainly try to.
The problem is once again cost and how we are going to finance it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the House for this opportunity to raise some questions with the minister. I will make a series of points and questions I would like the minister to respond to. I will try to do it very quickly.
One of the difficulties we have, as the House knows and the minister knows, is that the Standing Committee on Transport is unable to meet because of an impasse between the government and the opposition. The chief government whip is not allowing the committee to continue its work.
Normally after estimates are tabled all standing committees invite the minister they work with to come before them to discuss, as we are trying to do today, what do these figures mean, and what are the ramifications.
I wonder if the minister would be prepared to attend an unofficial meeting of the transport committee that my colleague from the Liberal Party and I will be arranging some time in the next couple of weeks. If the minister is agreeable, at his convenience, to come before all members, not just the opposition, but the government as well,
March 1, 1991

to talk to the minister about the matters in the estimates.
I have specific questions I want to put to the minister today. One of the big questions is about terminal 3. What is the Government of Canada gaining financially? I realize the minister may not have a specific dollar amount, but no one has been prepared to tell us what the deal is. Is it a percentage of gross revenue? Is it a percentage of net revenue, somewhere in between, or is it a fixed amount?
I think the people of Canada need to know, that in order to evaluate whether or not the principle of privatization, of private participation in a development and operation of airports is appropriate, irrespective of the philosophical differences that we may have in this House.
The other question ties into that, in terms of the devolution of airports. Can the minister indicate the department's projections as to what that is going to mean to the revenue side of the balance sheet for Transport Canada. If these airports are turned over, whether it is a private sector or a community or what have you, there obviously has to be some kind of new financial mechanism. What is it going to cost the system as a whole because, quite frankly, Pearson and Vancouver have been helping to cross-subsidize the operation at the other airports.
The one final question I would like to put at this point relates to the estimates. There seems to be an underlying erosion of the minister's tools for safety. For example, under surface and railway safety there is a decline of $3.2 million last year to this year. The Transportation Accident Investigation and Safety Board is getting less than a 1 per cent increase. Third, Marine Search and Rescue shows a $12.9 million decrease. I realize on this last one that it may be because of some kind of shuffle and perhaps the minister could indicate that.
But it seems to me that at a time when we are seeing higher instances of rail accidents, that we have an excellent working commission dealing with the Dryden inquiry that will report later this year and, in fact, its report may have some impact on the operation of the board, that one would assume that there needs to be dollars there to do the work.
The Budget
Madam Speaker, I know you are anxious to hear from the minister and so am I, so let me sit down and hear him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was just wondering how the minister would find time to answer all the hon. member's questions considering the time that was being taken to put the question.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is easy, Madam Speaker, I will just answer the easiest questions.
I do not want to interfere with the government whip's work on committees, so I think that both the government whip and the opposition whip-and my hon. friend is an opposition whip- can settle their differences quickly. I am always glad to come to committee and field the questions.
Let me just say this. Presently, Pearson produces financial statements so the hon. member can see the asset base. The operating statement is available to everybody. I would suggest to you that when the revenue from T-3 kicks in, it will show in the financial statements.
We have an agreement with the developer. It was part of the deal that the contract would be private between the government and the developer, but the money we get from T-3 will be shown in the financial statements of Pearson. So I think that will take care of that.
As far as the devolution of airports is concerned, what we intend to do and what we have been doing is saying that is the asset base, the taxpayers of Canada will get a return on their investment and then we want a cut of the action. We want a cut of the terminal development, the coffee shop and the land rentals. So the taxpayer is going to get out of the business of running airports. The government should not be in the business of running airports. We do not need the Minister of Transport and public servants to decide whether a room this size should be a coffee shop or a duty free shop. Some days it would make a good hangar. But it is not necessary for the government to do that. That is why we are transferring it. We are getting a percentage of the action on it. We have that bill before committee next week, and I will be glad to come to committee and answer any questions on that.
The last question was about safety. Safety is an absolute priority of Transport Canada. Any rearrangements of person-years and funding always bears in mind

The Budget
the fact that safety is a top priority. It will continue to be a top priority.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are here supposedly to deal with the Budget. But the fact is that we are here to deal with the government's ability-or total lack of it-to provide Canadian men and women with a sound and effective management of the economy.
On TUesday, the Minister of Finance presented the Seventh Budget of his government. For sure, it was not a lucky seven for Canadians.
Early in 1991, Canada's economic outlook is rather gloomy. I quote:
"We foresee that the Gross National Product will be down 0.3 per cent. Unemployment will reach 10 per cent. The economy will grow at a rate of about 0.9 per cent, its lowest level in the last decade. Our economy is sinking into a recession. For the past two years, the Minister of Finance has been telling us that the only way to fight inflation is to create unemployment. In this Budget, he is telling Canadians that they can expect one more year of the same. There is not one atom of a comprehensive economic strategy in this Budget. There is no overall vision, no indication that the government knows to where it is headed."
Madam Speaker, the reason our country's economy is ailing is that the government just does not know how to manage the shop. Over the past six years, the government could have used a number of positive factors to cure the economy.
The world economic growth-Six years of tax increases, six years of program cuts.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You are perfectly right to say shame.
In spite of that, the country is overburdened with debts as well as an enormous deficit. It is a shameful performance.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Indeed!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A shameful performance which is likely to continue if we accept this Budget. In short, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has lost his bearings.

When this government came to power, it had one goal: deficit reduction. It has failed miserably. Why? Because of its failure to understand that deficit reduction does not only come from cutting; it comes from growth, and growth comes from investment.
This government has consistently under-invested while other countries in the world, such as Germany and Japan, have invested. Those countries now prosper while Michael Wilson has brought this country to its knees. How? Let me count the ways.
Cutbacks in education. There is an inherent contradiction between this government's constant rattling on about its advocating competitiveness on the one hand and promoting policies on the other which must inevitably lead to cutbacks in education.
Twenty-five per cent of Canadians are functionally illiterate. We have, among the industrialized countries, one of the lowest rates of high school attainment. What is this government's answer to this? It is to make sure that every student who wants to go to university next year will have to pay up to $1,000 more.
It is about to cut out the support systems for single parent families who want to send their children to school. It is a failure to understand that the sinews of the nation are built on the nation's youth.
Cutbacks in social programs. This government's failure to invest in people perpetuates a cycle of poverty. The government fails to understand that a dollar invested in Canadians today will make you $5 later on.
Indeed, when I see this particular Speaker in the chair, it gives me some pleasure to raise the cutbacks in the environment. This government has just trashed the green plan. The green plan was not very good. It did not have much vision. There was not much of a message. There was not much in it, but it was the best this lamentable government could come up with and what it has now done is thrown it in the wastebasket.
The minister stood opposite me and told us how he was going to spend $3 billion over five years. He told us it had not only been approved but that it was committed. He virtually told us that it was a sacred trust. He has now announced a one third cut in the first year alone-$600 million over the next five years.
March 1, 1991

The government will tell us it is a deferment. That is guff. The green plan as presented by the minister was a rolling plan. More moneys were to be spent in the sixth year and in the seventh year. This is an absolute cutback of one third, $125 million in the first year alone.
Yesterday it was reported that the Minister of the Environment in scrum outside here said that industrial development was more important than the environment. Well, that is a statement which is as dated as the Edsel. It is an incredible statement. It is incredibly discouraging for those who believe in the environment to think that the Minister of the Environment would say it. It arises from a failure to understand that the environment is a moral value. It arises out of the failure of this government to understand that in the new economics you cannot have a sound economy in an unsound environment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Absolutely. Bravo.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank my colleagues. It arises out of a failure to understand that a nation is not growing because of its failure to invest in research and development. The environment and the development of environmental technologies represent one of the great growth industries of the future. This nation is now in a position where if it does not develop those technologies, in 10 years it will be buying them from the Germans and the Japanese, as it buys VCRs and record players today. But if this nation develops them today, then maybe it will develop a new industrial base. The environment is not a cost. It is a phenomenal opportunity for us to build a new economy.
This government's problem is that it fails to understand that the environmental deficit is an economic deficit. It fails to understand that the social deficit is an economic deficit. If there is any doubt about this, simply look at this Minister of Finance's record over the last seven years. In his time there has been a doubling of the deficit and it has arisen out of one thing: this government's failure to understand the necessity of investing in the future.
This budget contains many facets, all of them bad. I began by saying that we are not here to debate the budget. Indeed, we are here to debate this government's competence. I should have said we are also here to
The Budget
debate national unity. This budget represents the opening shot in the government's battle to hold the country together and it could not have been more inept. It could not have been more self-defeating.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How anyone could think that reneging on our commitments to the nation builds a nation is beyond me. The Tories will say that cutting payments for health and education improves the nation's finances. Well, that is garbage. The national debt is not only the federal debt, it is the federal debt in combination with the provincial and municipal debts. Shifting the debt burden does not solve our financial problems. In the end it is the same taxpayer who pays. But the way in which this government is going about it is weakening the sinews of the nation. Even more to the point, this government is repeating the mistakes it has made many times in the past, mistakes that have had a devastating effect on this nation.
In the free trade agreement this government, so desperate for a success even if it was only paper thin, and so afraid of failure, sat down cowardly with the Americans and gave up the ghost before the negotiations started.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It made every single concession. Every point it thought the Americans would raise at the table, it gave up before it got there, because this indeed is a craven government.
Then what happened with the Americans and the Canadians? John Crosbie stood up and said: "We have a great victory." It reminds me of peace in our time in 1938.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame. Yes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, it has just done the same thing. Now, as it prepares to sit down with a multitude of provinces across this country, this government is in the process of dismantling the nation so that there is nothing left to discuss, no bargaining chips on the table, and for those of us on this side of the House, those of us who believe in this country, it is beyond belief to stand here and watch what this government is doing with one of the nations that God put on this earth to fulfil great things.

March 1, 1991
The Budget
There is one man who must love this budget, and that is Jacques Parizeau, sitting there in his intellectual grey. He must be laughing all the way to the bank.
Well, there are other lessons that this government has not learned. In the course of the Meech debate, Canadians on either side of the debate said they wanted a public debate, they wanted to be consulted. But we sort of thought that the government would come to that conclusion itself with the formation of the Spicer commission. And yet, now before Spicer has returned, now before Gordon Smith and the federal bureaucrats have gone through their papers and presented them to the nation, this government blunders ahead with constitutional reform.
We do need a restructuring. It may well be that we are in 1865 and that great foresight is required. But, it will not be shown by this government.
There can be a no more manifest attack on national unity than the discriminating attack on certain parts of our country. My colleague from Newfoundland has spoken eloquently about this, as indeed have my other colleagues from the maritime provinces.
Let me speak a little bit about another part of the country that is suffering as a result of this budget. Quebec, Montreal, and you will forgive me but my own riding of LaSalle-Emard-
[Translation}
Ever since this government came into office, the economic situation in the Montreal area has been deteriorating. There is only one message in the Minister's Budget: Your are on your own! Good luck! With its fiscal policies, the government clearly indicates that it could not care less about Montreal's economic development.
All the same, my city is certainly the Mecca of Quebec entrepreneurship. It holds an enormous potential which could help Canada improves its competitive position. Unfortunately, the government stands idly by and allows a potential which a great many envy us to be wasted.
In Quebec, over the past 12 months, the number of personal bankruptcies has increased by 67 per cent and the number of business bankruptcies by 26 per cent. It is scandalous!
Last month, Montreal was the city which recorded the highest unemployment rate in Canada: 13.4 per cent.
The rate in Montreal East was over 20 per cent. The Tory government has abandoned Montreal and Quebec. Its policies have ruined one of the finest economic areas in the country.

I can see the clock is winding down, so just let me make one last remark in conclusion: Our country is in the throes of a national unity debate unseen before in our history. We are in the midst of a massive economic decline, permanent job loss and fundamental change far deeper than any of us ever anticipated, certainly far deeper than this government anticipated when only six months ago it failed to understand what everybody else in the world knew: Canadians were suffering deeply and the recession was biting hard.
This budget makes a bad situation worse. The continuation of high interest rate policies, the lack of decent adjustment programs, the continued strengthening of the Canadian dollar, all of which have crippled the nation, show on the part of this government a lack of economic and national understanding which is simply unforgivable.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Absolutely.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A nation needs national purpose. This budget represents national defeat. Let us in this House at this critical juncture of our country's history give the nation hope.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have to say I am always one to carefully follow the speeches of my hon. friend because his father, of course, was previously the member of Parliament for the area which I now have the honour to represent.
I do want to ask the member two or three questions. As I look back to the period of the last Liberal government that we had in this country, I see first an attack on the Public Service not much different from the attack that took place in this budget, the six and five program. I see, second, an approach to the tax system which built into that tax system a great many of the problems which we continue to attack the finance minister for today, such as the capacity for companies to borrow money here in Canada for activities any place throughout the world and to be able to deduct the interest costs of those funds from their taxes that they would otherwise have to pay
March 1, 1991

here in Canada, something which costs the ordinary taxpayer in this country a great deal.
I see as well a reduction, which the Liberals started, in the rates of income tax for higher income earners in this country-the 1983 budget of Marc Lalonde which brought tax rates for upper income earners from 42 per cent down to 34 per cent. Conservatives have taken that down to 29 per cent, which I am sure we both agree is unfortunate in terms of fairness in this country and in terms of a sense of national unity in this country.
What seems to me to have been the case in these three areas that I have cited, and I could cite many more, is that the Liberal Party started in the direction which the Conservative Party has followed. I want to ask the member whether he is, in making his strong plea for national unity in this country, saying that he will renounce and that his party renounces this past record of serving the privileged, of helping the wealthy, and of assisting the large-scare corporate sector in this country. Has there really been a case of the leopard changing its spots?

speechtext:

There are a couple of other things that I would like to say.
At the time the Liberal government brought in wage and price controls, inflation was triple, almost quadruple what it is today. The world was a far different world, and
The Budget
I am glad to say that it was Liberal policies-a far greater preference to absurd high interest rates that we have now-that brought the country back.
I would also like to say to this member that as I sit there watching the activities of Bob Rae in Ontario and I see as he reneges on election promise after election promise, when I see Bob Rae begin to retreat into a narrow little shell and that all the rhetoric that the NDP has stood for suddenly finds itself to be empty and worthless as he tries to grapple with the realities of government, I begin to understand what hypocrisy really is.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: I would also like to say to this particular member, as he asks the question "why should the Canadian government support Canadian companies that operate around the world ?", that he is indeed giving us an indication of how narrow the NDP thinking is. We Canadians are prepared to take on anybody. I think it is disgraceful that the NDP, so rooted in the orthodoxy of the 1930s, fails to understand that this country can compete with anybody. Again, with his business background, he would understand compound interest. We have been running deficits, but lower, for the first four years. The

compound interest on that debt amounts to approximately $120 billion.
The legacy that the Liberal government has left Canadians is a burden something in the order of $320 billion.
Now, he just spoke of hypocrisy in the other opposition party here. I would like him to comment on the scandalous out of control spending for 15 years. That is what Canadians are going to remember. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the member talks quite eloquently about compounding interest. What he really ought to understand is that what this government understands is compounding problems.
It is very clear how this country got into the soup. Following the free trade agreement-again, whether you were for the agreement or against the agreement-this government made a series of fundamental mistakes. I have been told by the Speaker that I must move quickly. Number one, no adjustment policies; number two, the government drove the dollar to 86 cents; number three, it drove interest rates up five points higher than the Americans and we were not able to compete, and you took us into this recession eight months ahead of the Americans, eight months. It is the first time and we are going to come out of it a year later.
We are in this because of the deliberate decisions of this government. The member knows it. Unfortunately, I am out of time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada has one of the highest standards of living in the world and a quality of life second to none.

We are indeed fortunate to be Canadians and to live here, Mr. Speaker.

But there is a battle that we have been fighting since 1984, a battle to restore health to our economy and to pull ourselves out of the hole the debt has dragged us
into. We are paying the price now over and over again for too many years of consuming more government services than we were willing to pay for and borrowing to make up the difference.
In 1984 the previous government handed out $1.33 in programs and services for every dollar it collected in taxes. Today our public debt is forecast to reach $400 billion by mid year, about $15,000 for every man, woman and child in Canada. The interest alone on the debt will eat up more than $43 billion, more than we spend on old age security, unemployment insurance and family allowances combined.
This cannot continue. As trustees for Canada's future, we must keep it strong and free for our children and all who follow.

Yet, Mr. Speaker, the 1991 Budget puts forward a plan for economic recovery. The Federal government wants to make the recession something of the past.

This budget will rebuild consumer and investor confidence and lead us into the environment of continuing growth and renewed prosperity. How can this be achieved? By creating the essential conditions for recovery. Increased spending will not create these conditions. Lower interest rates will. Lower interest rates will bring direct economic benefits to Canadian homeowners struggling to make their mortgage payments. At the current rate of about 12 per cent, a $100,000 mortgage with a 25-year amortization requires monthly payments of about $1,030. But the same mortgage at a rate of 9.5 per cent would require payments of about $850 a month, representing a savings of $180 a month or nearly $2,200 each year.
It is clear that for my constituents, living at the west end of Montreal, and for all new Canadian homeowners, our commitment, this government's commitment to lower interest rates, will be a direct economic benefit.
The plan for economic recovery is going to bring down interest rates by lowering inflation and by setting the government on course to balance its budget and reduce its borrowing.
The answer is not more spending. More spending would drive the interest rates up. The answer is lower spending and lower interest rates.
March 1, 1991

The new budget is quite simply an all-out assault on the deficit. All GST revenues will be used to service the debt. Grants to business and special interest groups will be cut by $75 million this year and $125 million next year.
The increase in cigarette taxes by three cents a cigarette will help keep the deficit down and, at the same time, discourage teenage smoking.
There will be no new income taxes, but unemployment insurance premiums will be increased to make sure this program pays its own way as required by law.
It is a tough plan. It is directed at the government, too. Ministerial salaries for the Prime Minister and all cabinet ministers will be frozen for a year. Members' and senators' salaries will again be increased by less than the cost of living. Senior management positions in the Public Service will be cut by 10 per cent.
Operating budgets will be frozen at current levels, and the government will legislate mandatory program spending limits.
This new budget plan will be tough on all governments, but we are not asking the provinces to do anything more than what we are doing ourselves. The 5 per cent growth limit on Canada Assistance Plan transfers to the wealthier provinces will be extended to 1994-95.
But, CAP contributions, these same contributions and equalization payments to less wealthy provinces, will continue to be exempt from budgetary controls.
The per capita freeze on established program funding announced last year will continue, but EPF transfers in total will continue to grow with the increase in population of each province.
Limits to the growth of transfers under EPF has raised concerns about the federal government's ability to continue enforcing Canadian national standards, particularly in medicare, under the Canada Health Act.
This has been addressed. Legislation will be introduced to ensure that the federal government continues to have the means to enforce these principles and standards. The commitment to medicare in Canada will not be compromised.
The Budget
Our battle is not only to restore Canada's economy, to bring about short term economic recovery, but to set the stage for a long term recovery assuring a stable and competitive economy, providing job opportunities for all who are ready to work.
All Canadians are in this battle. As the Minister of Finance stated in the House this week, there is too much at stake for anything less than a full national effort.
Yes, Canadians enjoy a quality of life second to none and we want to ensure that it stays that way.
