Mr. Speaker, I do enjoy listening to hon. members from the government side talking about the burden of the national debt. It seems they always like to go back to 1984 and talk about the deficit at that time.
I would like to remind the hon. member who has just spoken of a couple of things. First of all, his government came into office in September 1984. Shortly after that, the Minister of Finance projected in an economic statement in November the deficit for the year in which the government was elected, 1984-85.
By the end of March, he had exceeded his own forecast because he put every possible expenditure he could find and shoved it through the books of the country in that fiscal year. He still cites that as being the Liberal deficit.
Not only was that the case, but when he looks at the numbers, he will discover that more than half of the current national debt has been run up by the current government and the current Minister of Finance, almost $400 billion of debt, more than double what it was when he took office. That is from a government that was elected to bring down the debt.
I want to ask him to comment on two quotations that I am going to read to him. I would like him to say what he thinks about these views, which were expressed with respect to an economic statement at a time when the country was coming out of recession.
The first one is this, and I quote: "In this budget that the minister has just presented unemployment insurance premiums are going to increase by 40 per cent. That is purely and simply a tax increase. It is a tax increase when it can be least afforded and it is another colossal error".

March 1, 1991
The Budget
The second quotation is: "The minister announced a $500 million job-creation program. I guess we have to say, Mr. Speaker, it is a step in the right direction. They have addressed the problem of unemployment in this budget, but it is a very small step. Five hundred million dollars sounds like a lot of money, but it is $300 per unemployed worker and amounts to some one-quarter of one per cent of the total size of our economy today".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Just before recognizing the hon. member and giving him a chance to reply, may I inquire as to whether or not he is planning to use his full 20 minutes and a 10-minute question period, or is he sharing his time with someone else in light of the fact that he did not speak for the full 20 minutes?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I will be happy to provide that time to the other members.
My hon. colleague from the opposition has raised the question of the national debt. There is no question, as we spent and spent in the 1970s and early 1980s and came into a period of recession in the early 1980s, that the ability of the government to tax at the rate it was spending became impossible. It was totally non-political to consider taxing, but it was very political to consider spending.
Buying our way out of trouble was the in thing. The community that we are all part of in Canada became a me, me, me society. "Look after me". "Not in my backyard" was another expression we used to hear.
The real truth was that we became convinced we could afford anything. Suddenly, it became loud and clear that we were going into debt at such a rate that the debt would decide what we could do in the future. The size of the debt and the interest on it were the determining forces on whether or not we could include day care centres or service of all kinds of programs.
To not reflect on those years when we used to increase spending, on average I think the estimate was 13.4 per
cent per year, and brought it down to where in these last six years since our government was elected with an obligation to the voters of this country that we would attack the deficit and control the debt and manage the economy, we actually have increased our government expenditures at less than the cost of living, meaning we are constantly reducing the fat in government.
The fat can be overlap; it can be duplication. All of us know that between this level of government, the provincial level of government and the municipal level of government there are sometimes three agencies looking after the same service. The answer is that we must come together as a country and eliminate this kind of waste.
One way of promoting that kind of dialogue and that kind of resolution will surely be when we stop providing the money to be spent. The open-ended "you give away the service and we will pay for it" has to end. This government in these last two budgets has made it very clear that we are no longer going to spend for excess.
Let us get together. Somebody raised the question, I think it was the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard in his remarks earlier, that this kind of activity is going to break up Canadian unity. It is the one thing that gives our country the chance not to blow our opportunity through waste, duplication and overlap. Let us start bringing all provincial governments and all municipal governments into the same harness that says there are only so many dollars in the kitty, in the taxpayer's pocket. We cannot charge it to our grandchildren or their children.
I might answer the second question which was in the area of UIC. It is now becoming accepted that it needs to and, by law, must meet its obligations.
We are going through a period of recession. There are demands on those funds. They have to be met by law. But, there are already indications and forecasts from all kinds of sources that with the way in which this country is being governed, in comparison with our big neighbour to the south and all our other trading nations, we will be into a recovery before mid-year, or certainly into the early part of the second half of the year.
With those job opportunities, we will be back on the cycle we began in 1984, since when there have been
1,600,000	new jobs created, many of them out in the west end of Montreal.

Mr. Speaker, I thought that what the hon. member for Lachine-Lac-Saint-Louis, in Quebec, had to say was very interesting. During his speech on the Budget, he mentioned cigarettes. If I remember correctly, one of the major companies in the province of Quebec is Imperial Tobacco. Canada's heaviest smokers are probably in Quebec.
That being said, I want to get back to the cigarette issue. He seemed proud of the fact that the Conservatives were now going to take 3 cents more per cigarette from young people in Quebec and across Canada, every time they smoke a cigarette, which means 75 cents more per package.
He seemed to be proud of taking money from young people, because it hits them where it hurts. It takes two or three kicks to teach them how to do things properly. I can inform the hon. member that is not the way to explain cancer-related problems to children. If you are really interested in dealing with smoking, you should do a lot more research on cancer related problems. You should spend a lot more money on research and on publicizing the negative effects of cigarette smoking. You should spend more money on public education, to help people quit smoking gradually.
I repeat, kicking people in the pocketbook or in the face is not the way to correct their vices, if it is a vice.

Mr. Speaker, in response to the concern raised by the hon. member regarding the introduction of youngsters to the hazards of smoking, it is certainly primarily incumbant on parents or grandparents like me to promote caution.
In my youth, smoking was considered harmless. Today, its dangers are well known, as are the costs involved for every citizen once the habit is firmly rooted and the demands on our health care system to treat, patch up or save the smokers' organs. All that is known. By charging 75 cents more on each pack of cigarettes, we are giving a clear indication to our young people who have some financial means, yet limited, that we, in this country, want them to take a good hard look at that habit.
The Budget

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise before the House as the member for Winnipeg North and also as the Official Opposition critic for National Health and Welfare. I will therefore focus my debate on the budget in this area.
With this portfolio comes a responsibility to warn this government that its new budget will provoke the destruction of health care as we know it today. I am surprised the members of government need to be warned. The signs are all around them.
For months I have been watching the steam build on the issue of medicare. It started with the budget of last year, and then I saw Bill C-69, the complicated government expenditures legislation, slipped past this House and into the Senate and given Royal assent sadly early last month.
This Bill C-69 launched a critical government assault on medicare. As the social and health care groups across the country can attest, Bill C-69 is a deadly bill for health care and other social programs. It freezes and caps transfer payments, the amount transferred by the federal government to the provinces to aid medicare and post-secondary education.
With this freeze we will cripple medicare, we will cripple post-secondary education, and we will cripple other social programs.
And so the steam builds. Adding to the pressure was a particular meeting in the autumn of last year when western finance ministers grouped in Winnipeg, in my home city of Winnipeg. Something very significant happened at that meeting, something that will bear on Mr. Wilson's budget, on this government's budget.
The western ministers agreed the federal government should deliver transfer payments while relinquishing control over national standards of health care. They want a disentangling of federal funding and autonomy for health care policy in the provinces.
The steam builds under medicare.

March 1, 1991
The Budget
On December 7 last year came an announcement from the Minister of Health from Quebec that he planned to revamp his province's existing health care system. This included a $5 disincentive fee, which I prefer to call a user fee for non-essential visits to the emergency wards.
I do not blame Quebec. Provinces are being forced to take initiatives like this one because the federal government has been limiting its proper financial share of the implementation of medicare.
There you have it all. All the signs are before you, Mr. Speaker: the budget of 1990, Bill C-69, the threats by the provincial finance ministers, the flagrant disregard for the Canada Health Act, and failure on the part of this federal government to enforce that Health Act. All the signs, all this steam building under medicare-pressure, pressure, and more pressure.
Then three days ago the government delivered the fatal blow and this is not exaggeration. The fatal blow to universal health care came when Mr. Wilson skimmed an additional $2.3 billion from transfer payments to the provinces.
Did he not see the signs? Was he not forewarned of the volatile situation of health care? Why did he not move to protect the health care system instead of pummelling it with further cuts?
I cannot understand it. Our health care system is one of our most prized possessions of citizenship and now it is slipping from our grasp. Or should I say medicare is being tom from our grasp by this government?
I shake my head in wonder as I hear the government rationalize its decision. As the government says, and I quote:
Legislation will be introduced to ensure the federal government
continues to have means to enforce these national medicare
principles. The principles of the Canada Health Act will not be
compromised.
I believe the compromise took place long ago when in a Centre Block boardroom in this building, Mr. Mulro-ney and his ministers decided to whittle transfer payments down to the quick. Now they promise the new legislation, and I quote: "The principles of the Canada Health Act will not be compromised".
But I ask: Why is new legislation necessary? The current legislation enables the government to enforce the five cardinal principles of medicare: accessibility,
portability, universality, comprehensiveness and nonprofit public administration.
The key enforcement tool is the ability to cut transfer payments. That is in the Canada Health Act. How ironic that the government is bartering away its enforcement power. In the words of my colleague, my deputy leader: "He who pays the piper calls the tune".
Who will be calling the tune? Will it be the federal government or the provinces? Who will be dancing to it? The poor, the elderly, the children of poverty and the struggling middle class.
The weakness lies not in the Canada Health Act; the weakness lies in this Conservative government.
How can the Canadian people trust the word of this government as they are being asked to do? How can this government protect medicare?
Let me give you two examples of the deep concern the government holds for the principles of the Canada Health Act.
For years the citizens of Quebec have been denied portability, often paying out of their own pockets for health care received in other provinces. Has the federal government interceded on their behalf? No, instead, a blind eye has been turned to the situation. Quebec is forced to do this because the federal government is not doing its share.
Has the government intervened when Alberta and British Columbia charged all citizens, regardless of income, the same premium for health care?
No, it has not and it does not. People from those provinces who cannot afford their premiums are disallowed from visiting doctors and medical care must be received from the emergency wards.
The federal government has set the stage for a showdown between provinces and the Canada Health Act, and what a fight it will be. In one comer are the provinces, determined to win autonomy over health care. In the other comer, Mr. Mulroney, Mr. Wilson, Mr. Beatty, seemingly championing the cause of universal medicare.
Honestly, who do you believe will be victorious in this battle? If I were a betting man, I would not put my money on the triumph of medicare.
March 1, 1991

The provinces will undoubtedly win and leave that ring flanked by an entourage of extra billing and user fees. And medicare, which was promised by that great Liberal Prime Minister, Mackenzie King in 1919, would suffer defeat.
How long will it be before the provinces call the bluff of the federal government?
What have they to fear?
The minister of health for Quebec no longer believes the federal government will protect national health care standards. He stated that Ottawa has been reducing transfer payments to provinces, proving that the federal government can no longer afford universality of health care. This would suggest Mr. Cote believes that reduced transfer payments have exacerbated the stress to the health care system. He believes Quebec should make its own way and avoid federal government bungling.
Quebec's Intergovernmental Affairs Minister has said that government has no business dictating health care standards for his province and, to do so, is unconstitutional.
The Minister of Health for that province also said: "Certain provinces-''-and he was alluding to Alberta and British Columbia-"-have shown an interest in debating with the federal government the relevancy of some provisions of the Canada Health Act. We are one of the provinces and we will open the debate."
In 1946, another great Canadian, Tommy Douglas, introduced the Saskatchewan Hospitalization Act providing public insurance coverage for hospital care. Later, in 1966, the National Medical Care Insurance Act succeeded this legislation.
Eventually, posed by threats of extra billing and user fees, the Liberal government introduced the Canada Health Act. It was ushered in Parliament and passed in April, 1984 with the approval of all political parties and all Canadians. It has been a source of national pride. It is a solid piece of legislation and one that has the respect of the world. Our health care system is second to none. It belongs to all Canadians regardless of race, culture, place of residence or earnings. It should be protected and must be preserved.
The Budget
Instead, this federal government is eroding medicare away to nothing. The government will explain this away and patronize Canadians with the quotation: "You simply do not understand", and, "Let me explain one more time". But make no mistake about it, medicare is in danger.
Continually, the government points to the national debt as the reason for all the hardship in this new budget. I heard it today, I heard it yesterday and I have heard it many times. I am equally concerned about the national debt, but the total national debt is not the equivalent of per-person debt as this government would like all Canadians to believe. It is not. Eighty per cent of that money is owed to municipalities, provinces, other Canadian citizens and the Bank of Canada, and therefore as revenues to the government. Please remember that the debt has doubled since this government came into power. You cannot criticize the past when your own past is not as good.
The government also says the rising public debt is a growing concern, a cause for concern. I, too, believe the increasing public debt is a grave situation, but I must point out that the Tory government caused this recession which led to drastically increased bankruptcies which fed into the public debt and neither the public debt or deficit should be used as an excuse to deny funding to medicare.
The detractors point to our health care system and criticize. They say we already have too much, that we must learn to expect less from medicare and from the government. Well I have this response for them. It is easy to speak against medicare while you are healthy and wealthy. Not everyone, like members of Parliament, can be treated at the exclusive National Defence Medical Health Centre clinic, but if they had to join a queue for life-saving surgery or seek treatment in an overcrowded, understaffed health care facility their thinking might change.
Indeed, sometimes health care can mean the difference between poverty and prosperity. This morning, at the Canadian Medical Association Leadership Conference, a distinguished Canadian, a former member of this Parliament, the hon. Mitchell Sharp said:
I was saved from personal bankruptcy by a universal system of
health care.

March 1, 1991
The Budget
For most, the case is different. They will not miss medicare until it is gone.
Here in Canada, even before the newest funding cuts, people were dying while on waiting lists for surgery. This is shameful.
I ask the government to turn its attention to the hospitals closing beds due to lack of funds. Explain to patients and staff that transfer payment cuts are not a problem, that direct taxation by the provinces will fill the breach.
Meanwhile, our nurses and doctors are flocking to practice in the United States. American companies hand out glossy brochures displaying sunshine and smiles. Money is not an object, the way it is in our country, despite the fact that more of their Gross National Product goes to health care than any other country.
As our shortage of nurses becomes critical in Canada, we will see them disappear, beckoned south by higher wages and salaries that are commensurate with the respect they deserve.
Look south again for the services Canada has not the funds to provide: the state-of-the art cancer treatment centres; centres for rehabilitating victims of drug and alcohol abuse; facilities for children suffering from psychiatric illnesses.
These are just some of the services Canada cannot or does not provide its citizens fully.
There are other things as well. Treatment facilities for new diseases and for the elderly. We lack new technology and laboratory equipment, and its purchase is becoming an impossibility.
These are the problems with health care now, today: beds closing, inadequate care and stressed health care professionals. How can funding cuts be justified?
There is an old saying that goes like this: "If you have not got your health, you have not got much." How true.
Unfortunately, medicare will collapse into a state of extra billing and user fees. A two-tier system of health care will develop. The rich will be segregated from the poor by expense and privacy, while the poor languish in over-crowded, sub-standard hospitals and clinics where health care professionals struggle to accommodate them.
This is not fear-mongering. This is the reality we face if health care is not made a top priority by government.
Yes, we have the verbal reassurances, the confident answers that seem to rise with ease from this government in trying to quell the fears of Canadians.
On December 3, the Minister of Finance said: "We have no intention of relinquishing any sense of responsibility we have for the National Health Act. We have every intention of continuing to assist provinces and in particular, assist those provinces that are low-income provinces to assure that they can continue to provide the services that are available in the wealthier provinces of the country."
That same day, the Minister of Health said that no changes to the Canada Health Act were being contemplated.
Yesterday afternoon in this House, under question by my colleague, the Liberal finance critic, the Minister of Health in reply declared that Canadians had a choice between "debts, higher taxes and cuts". He said what threatens Medicare is "the interest being paid on the national debt".
In a recent interview on nursing published today, Mr. Beatty denied there is a crisis in nursing and said: "The strain on the health care system is a symptom of our success. The birth rate is low and the elderly are living longer".
I guarantee you, 1.5 million unemployed and more than 1 million children living in poverty are not the hallmarks of success.
We have been reassured again and again and again by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance that health care is not in danger. Now, we are assured freezing transfer payments is the lesser of three evils: cuts, debt and higher taxes.
In fact, the Liberal Party has been accused by this government of scare-mongering and of misrepresenting the facts for pointing out that health care is being disassembled piece by piece. Well, in the remaining minute, no matter how you analyze the issue, these cuts and freezes and caps are hurting medicare. Not only are they destroying medicare, but they are crippling Established Programs Financing.
March 1, 1991

Did you know, Madam Speaker, that within the budget there was no mention of child poverty or day care? And $100 million were taken from the job creation fund.
The poor are met with cuts or contempt, enclosed in a thundering silence from this government that does not care for them and does not care at all.
Yesterday, I had a call from Joanne Oberg of the Canadian Day Care Advocacy Association. She asked my staff if they knew of cuts being made to her program, which is partially funded by the Minister of State. The government's promised universal day care program was a fleeting election fantasy, now replaced by an impending threat that even day care organizations will be cut off. Again, who will be hurt by this? Those who have the least.
I must again reiterate the fact that there was no mention, not one word, in the budget of a strategy for child poverty and how to solve it. When will the government move on this issue? Why does the government not take revenue from the GST, which we oppose, if the revenues will be there and apply it to our future, our children? Children cannot eat line graphs on inflation and promises of decreased debt. All the talk and rhetoric from this government will not make them grow strong and healthy. They need immediate help now. It is deeds, not words, on which this government will be judged by all Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I just happened to hear from the hon. member from Edmonton that there are a few pigs out there. The hon. member for pigs. I do not know what this man is really referring to, but he may want to get up and make a speech on it.
I would just like to make a comment and ask the hon. member from Winnipeg who spoke of the dire straits that the Liberal Party finds now in this country since the Conservatives have been in government. Apparently, listening to what the gentleman said, the country has deteriorated in its ability to deal with health problems because of the finance minister's budget. There is, he said, some indication that we have nothing but poverty among our children of Canada, as if you go down the street and they are all holding out a little can for food aid.
The Budget
If you listened to the member from Winnipeg, he painted a picture of this country just being in total despair as a result of this government. Yet, he also believes that if the Liberals were in power, they would address the dire needs of this country. He made no mention at all of the tremendous growth in the economy and in the way government dealt with a severe deficit when we took power in 1984. He does not even wish to consider that as an area of concern by the party of which he is a member.
I would like to ask the member from Winnipeg, just what does he see as the answer to this severe problem of poverty in children and homelessness? Is it to spend $1 billion, $2 billion or $3 billion or $5 billion at this time, to borrow the money to overcome that problem? Is that his party's answer today, to spend more money? And, by doing that, would his finance critic stand up in the House six months from now and say: "This government has allowed the deficit to grow", and criticize the very government that he would ask to spend the money? These are the questions that he has not answered in his condemnation of the finance minister's budget, and I would like to hear what he has to say in that regard right now.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is regrettable that the hon. member was late in coming in because I did indicate and I tell this government that you cannot equate the total national debt as the equivalent of a person-to-person debt, because only about 20 per cent of the total national debt is owed to foreign people in foreign currency.
When you pay interest and principal to the Bank of Canada, that is revenue for the government of this country, so do not mislead all Canadians. They are more intelligent than you think.
I am very serious. If they would care to go to the Library of Parliament and research, read some excellent works on economics by a professor at the University of Manitoba, they would have no basis asking and commenting this way.
Second, the hon. member from Portage asked if I would borrow money, as though borrowing money for a good cause is bad. When children are sick, would you let them go and die and be hungry in their stomachs only because we would like to allocate money for military arms, for CF-18s, the nuclear submarine program that

The Budget
we asked be scrapped, and it was scrapped because once you listened to us.
Borrowing and investing in the future of our country is not deficit, it is investment. How can you say that you would like to be competitive and then reduce transfer payments for education, and then make it difficult for our young people to learn? They may even die and you want them to be competitive. You want them to develop expertise. I cannot understand this member's understanding of health care at all.
What would I do? I would establish a policy of full employment for this country. I would increase the minimum wage for federal civil servants. That is how you solve poverty.
I would end my answer to the hon. gentleman by saying that denying that problems exist is not the way to solve the problem. Denying that poverty exists is not the solution to the problem of poverty. Denying that there is a crisis in the health care system is not the way to solve the crisis in the health care system. I am reminded due to my medical background that denial on the part of a patient is not the way to participate in treatment.

speechtext:
I think all Canadians know that the New Democratic Party is the party that was responsible for the birth of medicare in Canada with Tommy Douglas taking the leadership in Saskatchewan against tremendous opposition, including the opposition of doctors who went on strike, like my colleague who just spoke, against medicare.
When national medicare was brought in, it was a partnership between the federal and provincial governments, a 50-50 partnership, and that partnership carried on until it was smashed by the Liberal government. In 1977, when the established program funding was introduced, it was to get away from the cost-sharing of a 50-50 partnership.
I would like my hon. colleague to say how come it was the Liberals who started backing away from the 50-50 partnership. First of all in 1982, when Allan MacEachen, that famous person in that other place, ended the revenue guarantee. It cost the provinces $1.2 billion in lost revenue by 1984, $1.2 billion that the Liberals took out of national medicare by 1984. In addition, the six and five program took another $250 million out of post-secondary education.
The precedents for the smashing of the partnership between the provinces and the federal government were put in place by the Liberals. The foundation for the devastation of medicare that the Tories are now going forward with was developed by the Liberals.
I would like the hon. member to explain how he can now stand up and criticize the Tories for doing exactly what the Liberals did.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, one of the points that came home to me very strongly as I talked to people, without them knowing that I was a member of Parliament, was the fact that they think that what we get into in this House is really a bunch of silliness. People are truly fed up with the way the minute the television camera hits us, we all start to act as if we were Clark Gable. It really is a tendency, and I am not criticizing anyone else any more than myself, because that is the reality of what we do. The minute television hit the House of Commons, we all became actors and the power had to leave. The decisions are now made in committees, where we do not have television, because we cannot seem to address the issues in a sensible way.
What I would like to try to do today is to say a few words about the reality of the situation. If I had any goal, it would be to try and face the world as it is today and have Canadians who might be listening this afternoon realize that the budget has to be seen in a broader Canadian context and, indeed, in a global context.
The opposition parties, of course, will adopt the strategy that we used in opposition. It is a strategy of trying to pick out little parts of the budget and blow it up as if it were the most important part of the budget, rather than seeing everything in a broader context. That is a very clever debating strategy, and we all do it. But I think the citizens out there often forget that that is the debating strategy and the tactic that the opposition parties use, and quite properly use.
I think Canadians are beginning to realize, too, the awesome power that special interest groups have come to hold in our country. I can say as an elected person over the last 12 years that the growth of the special interest groups and their power to virtually force us to make decisions in their favour rather than in the common good of the nation as a whole is very disturbing. I honestly do not know what the answer is. It is much worse in the United States of America, where individual congressmen are virtually captured by what they call PAC groups-personal action committees-which pay them a lot of money and get them re-elected. We do not
The Budget
have that problem to the same extent here because we use financing through the tax system. I think that is an excellent system and we want to keep that up because it puts more distance between us and the special interest groups. Nonetheless, the combination of a powerful special interest group and the national media, as we all know as members, here in Ottawa is totally isolated from the reality of Canadians who live in each of our individual ridings.
We are all very happy with our regional media who try to give some balance and are much better in giving both sides of the story than the national media. The national media seems intent on bringing down a Prime Minister or a government of whatever stripe is here. It is as if the national media believe that they are the opposition of the country and have a credibility or have the right to destroy people. They will destroy anybody in this House if they can get anything on you with absolute immunity. That is not right, but again with this concept of freedom of the press, I myself do not know how we can control it. I know that it is at the point where we have got to do something to bring that into a better system of balance.
What is the context of this budget and the government policy in general? I think again we have to understand the world as it is. There have been enormous changes in the world in the last 5, 10, 15 years. For example, in the European Economic Community we find this veiy powerful grouping of the European nations. It will be a common market by next year and they will have fewer barriers regarding the transfer of goods, capital and labour between sovereign nations than we have between our 10 provinces in this country.
Just think about it. Less than 50 years ago they were at war with each other and killed millions of themselves in that Second World War. Yet today they have fewer barriers regarding the transfer of goods, capital and labour, between the sovereign nations than we do here in Canada.
The think tanks, or the economic groups, tell us that there are some 1,600 barriers between the free transfer of goods within this country. In agriculture alone there are something like 160 barriers to the so-called Canadian common market. What that means is that as a nation we have not been able to compete with the other countries in the world.

The Budget
Then look at Asia. Look at that ASEAN group with Thailand, Brunei, Singapore and Malaysia. They again are into a common market that is very big; over 300 million people and the free transfer of goods, capital and labour.
We had to do something in this country because we are 24 million people. We are not isolated in the world. It is true that our dairy industry operates only for the Canadian market. It is true that the poultry industry and the feathered industry operate only for the Canadian market. But virtually every other aspect of agriculture-beef and grain, our forestry industry, our mining industry- creates wealth for us and has to compete in the world. Therefore, we have to meet that global situation. Whether it is with our tax system, whether it is with our free trade agreements, or whether it is with the tariff system, we have to be able to get on and compete in the world. That competition is fierce.
Privatizations; countries around the world of whatever political stripe, New Democratic, Liberal, Conservatives have all moved to privatizations. Why have they done that? Simply because it has been shown by just hard day-to-day evidence that nationalized companies cannot keep up in the marketplace. They cannot make those competitive decisions fast enough. They cannot deliver the goods. Partially, the reason is that when they are controlled politically, when they get into trouble, rather than making the proper decisions within their corporate context, they come to governments and governments bail them out. Again, as a special interest group, when they come in and say to us "If you do not give us this money, we are going to lay off 10,000 employees", of course we give them the money. Other countries have done that around the world. The solution has been to privatize, get the company out where politics cannot play a role in it and distort it.
What is the marketplace? It really is simply the sum total of all the individual decisions that Canadians make and people in other countries make.
That amounts to the marketplace and we believe fundamentally, or certainly I do, that millions and millions of individual decisions taken in the best interests of individuals themselves will lead to a far wiser result over all than if a government cabinet of whatever political stripe-it does not matter to me whether it is
Conservative, Liberal, or NDP-makes them. I just know from my life experience that governments cannot make those decisions to replace the millions of individual decisions that people make in their own interest.
The Liberal Party once believed that, and then under Prime Minister Trudeau it got off on a different track where it was much more socialist. The NDP is still, at the national level anyway-they are much more realistic at the provincial level where they have actually have had to exercise power-locked into the ideology of centralization. The NDP still wants to nationalize banks, to nationalize the CPR, and to nationalize the distribution of farm products.
I think the NDP will gradually get away from that. I hope they will in their next national policy conference. The fact of the matter is that social democratic countries across Europe are getting rid of their manufacturers' sales tax which we finally have, they are recognizing the rights of intellectual property.
Just think of the battle we had over the patent legislation on drugs. No doubt some years ago the drug companies were increasing the prices higher than they ought to have and so nations reacted. Other countries put in price review boards. What did Canada do? We took away their patent rights. So why would a company do any research and development in Canada? Of course, it would not. It would do its research in Germany, in Britain, in Switzerland, the United States where it could get a patent right.
When we tried to give patent rights here and instead substitute a prices review board we had an awesome fight. The NDP was instrumental in opposing that and held it up for many months.
It was the same with plant breeders' rights for agriculture. Other countries moved to plant breeders' rights 15 years ago. I can remember Eugene Whelan bringing in plant breeders' rights. We were in favour of it but the NDP and a number of church groups were opposed. They actually held up that bill for 15 years. By the time we brought the bill through, Canada and its young researchers are 15 years behind.
Fortunately, I have to say, they learned their lesson because when we came to the Integrated Circuits Intellectual Property Bill, to give patent rights to the people who design these chips and the way these microchips work, both opposition parties were in favour of that. But
March 1, 1991

they delayed the drug patent bill, they delayed plant breeders' rights.
Yet social democratic countries around the world adopted them years ago, 15 years ago. Why is it that Canada has to be so far behind? That is what has hurt us. We are behind. As a developed country we should be ahead. We should be leading the charge, not following along behind.
I have mentioned a number of things, for example, the GST. That fundamental move to replace a tax on our manufacturers, again other countries around the world had a manufacturers' sales tax and abandoned it years ago, but not Canada. We hung on to it and hung on to it, partially because this House has become stymied in being able to act quickly enough. Finally it has been replaced and we are joining the world community of nations in having a consumption tax. It is far better to tax consumption-people who consume more pay more-rather than taxing savings because it is the savings in a nation that are used to build its plants. It is savings that are used to refurbish plants, to move into new industries.
We have even got away from that. We were spending our savings on consumption. We were spending our savings by giving it to provinces, for example, the Canada Pension Plan. There is a contrast between the Quebec Pension Plan, where those premiums are taken and put into investments to build their province, and as a result Quebec today has a very dynamic small business industry, and the Canada Pension Plan, which was given to provinces at a very low rate of interest and they spent it on operating programs. As a result we have had to borrow money. We have a national debt of $400 billion of which half is owed offshore. We are totally captured by the capital markets of the world.
The new budget-the reality of 1984.
I want Canadians to appreciate the significance of 1984 and that budget deficit of $38 billion because it had two components to it. One component was the operating deficit and that was some $16 billion. What that meant was that Canadians were receiving $1.33 worth of programs. They were only being taxed $1 and the government was borrowing the rest under the table.
The Budget
Now for the individual it looked good. They had these wonderful programs. We love them. We were only taxed a dollar so we still had lots of money in our pockets. What did we do? We went out and paid too much for our houses, we paid too much for our farms, we paid too much for our businesses. So that in the area where I come from, land that was valued at about $100 per acre, based on its productivity, suddenly went up to $600. Of course, it could not continue on that basis because $600 land cannot be paid for with the produce it produces.
So, naturally, those are the farmers today who are in trouble, the people who bought that land for $600 an acre in my hometown, when it was really worth $100. That was all a result of receiving $1.33 in benefit programs and being taxed only $1 and the government borrowing the difference on the side, so to speak, or practically under the table. So the national debt started to grow.
When we came to power, we had a $38 billion deficit; $16 billion on the operating and $22 billion already for interest on that national debt.
Could the government change that around in one year? Well, anyone with any common sense knows that it cannot do that. It cannot increase taxes by $16 billion in one year and cut programs by $16 billion. We had to come up with a staged program. The first goal was to balance the operating budget, and our Minister of Finance did that in five years. It went from a deficit of $16 billion to, today, a surplus of $12 billion.
What that tells us is, if past governments had not built up the national debt, we could, this year in this budget, reduce taxes by $12 billion. Every cent of the deficit today is interest on the national debt. It was unnecessary because when Mr. Trudeau came in, indeed, Mr. Turner was the Minister of Finance who had a surplus budget. He started us into that routine of deficits and every year for 15 years the operating budget went up by 14 per cent. The Liberals did not have the honesty, I think, to turn to Canadians and say "look, you want this program, fine, here is a corresponding tax to pay for it".
If we could just put an amendment in our Constitution that governments had to say "for this program there is the tax, what is your choice", that would force a lot of

The Budget
restraint on governments and save people from getting into this long-term trap.
The people who should be really annoyed are the young Canadians. It is the young Canadians who see in this budget, for the first time, some hope. First of all, we are going to start to pay. Our generation is going to have to pay for these programs that we are using today. We are going to have to pay the taxes to not only cover our programs today, and we do, but we have an extra $12 billion in taxes to go toward interest on the national debt.
With the GST, by 1994, if everything works out, and nobody can guarantee that it will-but it is a reasonable plan and the past plan, to take the $16 billion deficit on operating to a $12 billion surplus, worked-we hope that by 1994 we will be equal. We will not have to borrow in the markets. Would that not be marvellous, that the federal government would not have to go out and borrow new money from Canadians. Then that money could be available for developing the economy and doing what Canadians want.
Then, what also happens is, as we pay a dollar down on the national debt at that time, we do not have to pay interest on that dollar the year after and we can get it going in an upward spiral so the more we pay on the debt, the more interest we have, we can then pay more on the national debt. It will be marvellous, but it is going to take 15 to 20 years because you cannot get yourselves into trouble over 15 years and get out of it in one or two years. It will probably take 15 years before we are out of it, but hopefully the national government will stick to that plan so we do not back off.
What I thought I would do with my remaining time is talk to Canadians who might be listening today about some of our programs. The Established Programs Financing transfers from the federal government some $20 billion to the provincial governments. When the opposition says that medicare is being destroyed, that is that tactic of trying to take one thing and trying to put some fear into Canadians, but it is not really based on reality. Twenty billion dollars a year is still being transferred to the provinces for medicare.
The reason medicare is in trouble goes back to that original program where the federal government was transferring money to the provinces, and the provinces were using it without being accountable. That is the fundamental problem that we have to solve. The people who spend the money should also have to tax for it, because they were getting the money, using it, but not giving any credit. We were taking on the national debt but they were spending the money.
In my home city of Lethbridge we have two huge hospitals. When you go out and look at all the little surrounding towns, you see every surrounding town has a hospital. We have not applied our medical capital well. We could have done it better and should have done it better. It is clear to us now but we have all these buildings. We have people working in all the buildings. How do you get rid of them?
It is the same with post-secondary education. The federal government pays an enormous percentage of the post-secondary education operating costs across the country. We get absolutely no credit as members of Parliament, nor do we get any say. At least in health care we have these five comprehensive conditions that we can hold up to a greater or lesser degree. In post-secondary education we have nothing. The federal government should have much more say in post-secondary education because it could then direct it in the national interest of Canada in order to compete with the other countries of the world.
I see my time has expired. I would love to go on for another half hour because I have many things I would like to put out by way of my point of view.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I enjoyed the words of the hon. member opposite. I know he has been here for quite a while and I thought he would be getting educated each year, but he seems to be going in the reverse direction.
He talked about our party being honest with the people and, if we did not have the money to spend for the programs, we should have told Canadians that. I was wondering if he could explain to the House and to Canadians why his party, in the first year of office, spent $34 billion over revenues that it took in? Why were they not honest and why did they not Canadian people: "Sorry, this is $34 billion we do not have and we cannot spend"? It would have been at that time, six years ago,
March 1, 1991

that the annual deficit and the public debt would have started going downhill and have not gone from $177 billion to $400 billion. I would like his explanation on that.
I would also like his explanation about the hospitals and post-secondary education. I do not know what he is recommending. Is he recommending that we eliminate the hospitals from small towns? Is that what he is suggesting? Yes, maybe the hospitals should be more efficient. I guess that is the Tory philosophy, yes. They are closing post offices so they want to close hospitals too.
He also mentioned that the federal government does not get any credit for post-secondary education. I disagree with him. The more students we graduate and at a higher level, the more we all get credit: the entire country, the nation. And we become more competitive.
I do not know what kind of credit he is talking about, that this x number of dollars came from the federal government and so that is our credit. Is he not forgetting that there is only one taxpayer in Canada? And, regardless of whether it is the federal, the provincial or the municipal government which takes it out of the taxpayer's pocket, it is still the same taxpayer that has to pay for that post-secondary education and for the hospitals. Are they trying to deceive the public by cutting the transfer payments to the provinces, making the provinces the fall guys and they are going to be the good guys saying "look how we have reduced the deficit", but not looking at the number of students who now cannot finish university or the number of people who cannot get hospital care because they have to wait and wait?
I used to enjoy the hon. member's speeches when he first arrived here, but something is happening to him and I do not like the change.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to respond, because in my comments I gave the answer to his question. He would have liked us to balance the budget in one year, in 1984. That is what he is saying.
The Minister of Finance was honest with Canadians. He said: "Look, we have this $38 billion deficit. There is $16 billion on the operating program and $22 billion in interest on the debt". We did not believe we could turn that around in a year, but we do have an economic recovery plan that he set out very carefully, an agenda
The Budget
for economic recovery that had over a period of years the solution to it. We have taken that operating deficit of $16 billion and turned it into a surplus of $12 billion. That is a major step ahead.
In another two or three fiscal years, we will have it so that we will not even have to borrow for the interest on the debt. That will be another milestone in this nation.
It is true that we will have basically a balanced budget in terms of financial requirements, but we will have a national debt perhaps even as high as $500 billion. It is only from that time that we can start to pay down the national debt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I keep hearing from the opposition side about cuts in the transfer payments.
I would like to hear from the member for Lethbridge if he has a list of figures to substantiate or refute the accusation of how badly we have kept to our transfer payments.
Does he have something to say, for instance, on the elderly? Does he have an idea or figures that could show from 1984 to the present time how the elderly have fared through the transfer payments? Does he have any kind of a list?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, I do, Madam Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A well researched manual.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My colleague knows that I speak out on other occasions and she agrees with me that it is a good point to make.
If you listen to the opposition you would think there had been cuts to everything. When I look at the figures for 1984, compared to 1991,1 do not see that at all. Look at the transfers to individuals. Elderly benefits in 1984-1985 were some $11 billion. This year it is $19 billion. That is not a cut; that is a massive increase of $8 billion.
I will move to another one: equalization. In 1984-1985 the equalization payments were $5.3 billion. This year they are $8.4 billion. That is an increase; that is not a cut. TUming to Canada Assistance, $3.7 billion then; now it is $5.6 billion.
If we look at natives, they received $1.2 billion in 1984, and this year it is $2.8. Of course it is being wisely spent.

There are now over 18,000 natives in post-secondary education. It was not anywhere near that back in 1984.
I came to town here with all of the prejudices and the myths that we learned at our grandfather's knee. One of those realities was that regional spending was not as high then. This is the transfers on regional and science, $1.4 billion. This year it is $2.6 billion. I am immensely proud when I go home to able to say to my neighbours: "Look, here is what it was in 1984 and here is what it is today". While we have increased the program spending to seniors, we have been able to decrease the federal budget, the deficit, and the national debt that will be on the heads of our children.
Turning to agriculture, which is critical for many of us including the member for Essex-Windsor, the amount the federal government spent on agriculture in 1984 was $707 million. This year it is $2.8 billion. That is not a cut; that is an increase of enormous proportions. I thank my colleague for giving me the opportunity to express that view.
The last one would be just even as a percentage of program spending. In 1984 the transfer payments to individuals were some 29 per cent. This year it is 35 per cent. So we have made some very fundamental shifts. We are transferring more federal dollars to individuals.
If I had my way, we would not spend one cent on a province. We would give all of our hospital dollars to people. We would give all of our post-secondary education dollars to students and let them make the choices as to what university they went to. That is what I would do.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very happy to be able to rise this afternoon and speak on the budget on behalf of the New Democratic Party. Because I am the critic for health I wish this afternoon to focus mainly on medicare as it is outlined in this budget.
I think that initially we have to take our minds back to how medicare was bom in Canada. First of all, of course, medicare came out of Saskatchewan with Tommy Douglas and the CCF. They fought against tremendous odds, tremendous power groups, including a doctors' strike, to bring in medicare. Without that determination and philosophical commitment to a universal, free and accessible medicare by Tommy Douglas and the CCF, we would not have medicare in Canada.
The whole question of the national medicare program was developed on the basis of a 50 per cent partnership between the federal government and the provinces. It came out of the Hall commission in 1964.
One of the things I do not understand about the Tories is that they appointed Emmett Hall. He was their person and he came across with the concept of a partnership in medicare, a partnership between the provinces and the federal government. He decided there would be a 50-50 partnership in financing, in responsibility for ensuring the health of Canadians, for innovation in terms of delivery of our health care and in research.
Medicare has been one of the national programs that has held this country together. It is based on a partnership, an equal commitment by the federal government and the provinces. That has held and has been a unifying force in this country.
What we have now is a unilateral decision by this government and by the preceding Liberal governments to dissolve the partnership, to simply say, "We are not going to meet our end of the bargain. We are not going to assume our responsibility. We are simply going to walk away from this partnership".
March 1, 1991

It is clear that Canadians realize what is happening to our medicare system. I would like to quote from the Canadian Medical Association. It said that it is alarmed at the decision to dismantle Canada's national medicare program. The Government of Canada is financially strangling medicare. This is from the same people who initially fought medicare.
We have the National Council of Welfare saying that it has grave concerns about the future of medicare. The freeze on Established Program Financing could mean the death of medicare as a national program by 1996.
What we have is a systematic erosion of our medicare system starting with the Liberals and being accelerated by the Tories since 1984, reductions of projected transfer payments in 1986, in last year's budget and now. What does this mean in terms of loss of revenue to the provinces?
The accumulated loss of revenue to the provinces is now $29.4 billion until the year 1994-95-that is $29.4 billion. It is not to the wealthy provinces alone. It is to some of the provinces that right now cannot afford to provide health care. Provinces like Newfoundland are going to lose $900 million.
British Columbia, my own home province, is going to lose $5 billion. I come from the riding of Surrey North where we have a dramatic shortage of hospital beds, one third the number that is necessary. This government has strangled our ability to develop new hospital beds.
Saskatchewan is going to lose $1.5 billion. By removing the ability to finance medicare, this cut is the strangulation, there will be an end of the cash.
The Tories have been trying to tell us for the last several months that that is not true. Last fall when I asked these questions the health minister and the finance minister denied it was going to happen. Now they are admitting it is going to happen.
It is going to happen as early as 1994 to 1995 for the large provinces. Of course, what does the Minister of Finance do in his budget? He says: "Don't worry. We will insist on national standards although the money will not be there to be transferred. We will bring in new legislation under the Fiscal Arrangements Act to ensure that the provinces comply with the Canada Health Act."
The Budget
I would like to inform them that Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario receive no money under equalization payments. How are you going to insist that B.C. comply with the act when they do not? The only other large chunks of transfer money that the government has is under the Canada Assistance Plan. Can you tell me on that side that if a province is not complying with the Canada Health Act, which you have never enforced before, you are going to stand up and take away moneys for child abuse, foster care from the Canada Assistance Plan because they are not complying with the Canada Health Act?
We have a national unity crisis right now. If the government does that with one of the provinces, taking money away from children because there is no compliance with the Canada Health Act, there would be a total disintegration.
One of the real problems with this budget is that it is a budget which destroys some of the programs that hold this country together, particularly our national medicare program.
The federal government cannot say: "We will call the tune but we will not pay the piper". That is what this budget says: we will stop cash transfers within four to five years, but we are still going to call the tune. That is just not going to happen within the framework of Canada. I think this type of legislation which destroys our national program-that is universally looked upon as one of the best health care systems in the world-is not the way to build national unity.
What is the excuse? The excuse that Tories give is the deficit. I agree that we have a deficit problem.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But you want to ignore it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I do not want to ignore it; I am not like the Tories. What we have had in ten years is a bungling Liberal administration which drove this country into one recession in 1982-83, and a bungling Conservative administration which drove this country into a recession in 1990 and 1991.
Yes, there is a deficit, and the deficit is caused by the Tories high interest rate policy, which is costing us $16 billion extra this year in interest payments alone, because our interest rate should be four percentage points lower-$16 billion because the Tories refused to tax their friends fairly. They gave tax concessions to the large

multinational corporations, tax concessions to the wealthy, those people earning $100,000 or more. They will not bring in fair taxation.
Those two things have caused the deficit. They are the main reasons this country is in this position now. If they had brought in fair taxation in 1984, the day they arrived, if they had brought in proper interest rates, we would not be running a deficit of $30 billion this year.
I am beginning to wonder what is behind it. And I think it is that the Tories are philosophically against universal social programs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Absolutely.

speechtext:
Absolutely. They want an Americanized system. They want this harmony with the United States that they keep talking about in the free trade deals, harmony with the American medical system, where 57 million Americans either have no medical insurance or are under insured.
Walter Cronkite has done a comparison between the two medical care systems. If you watched the program, you saw the difference. What is going to happen with this approach to our national medicare is that we are going to abandon it as a national program; instead of a blanket, we are going to get ten patchwork quilts. The provinces are going to start, under financial pressure, bringing in user fees, extra billings, a two-tiered health care system.
We already have people in British Columbia, such as the premier of B.C.-that great and fantastic thinker, and I say that a bit facetiously-who was talking about perhaps establishing private-for-pay health care for the people who can afford it. Maybe we should have the Americanization. That is what is going to happen if the federal government abandons its partnership.
In closing, Madam Speaker-I think my ten minutes are up. Are they not?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will be speaking for 20 minutes. I am glad there is a consensus in the House that I will now speak for 20 minutes.
The program that Walter Cronkite narrated was a very well documented and thoughtful program. He documented the problem of the American health care system, and some of the problems of the Canadian health medicare system. One of the things we have to realize is that there are problems within our Canadian health care system. There is no doubt we have problems we must address. They are the problems of escalating costs and a lack of distribution of health care across this country by region. There are problems that relate to access, and I want to spend a few minutes on each of those areas.
One of the things we have to start looking at is the federal government's role in looking at alternatives within our health care system.
The federal government has had a major responsibility for promotion and research in health care. It is the level of government that has supposedly been responsible for doing the research that is necessary to innovate within our health care system. It is the level of government that is supposed to be looking at health promotion, such things as anti-smoking campaigns, campaigns for promoting fitness and activity, campaigns which relate to abuse of drugs.
What has the government done in this budget? It slashed its expenditures in these areas, even in areas such as health services and promotion. Grants to voluntary health organizations have been held even, no increase. Grants to support health promotion at the community level have been cut by over 20 per cent.
This is the government's commitment to health promotion. It is the area that we need most. The government is refusing to deal with such issues as the promotion of adequate drug abuse programs, the whole promotion of the health problems of tobacco. The tobacco lobbyists are still preventing this government from bringing in realistic warning legislation dealing with smoking. It is simply because of the financial clout that some of the tobacco lobbyists have with this government.
The other area I want to address does not deal specifically with the question of medicare but with the budget is the reduction in the Canada Assistance Plan.
There is a tremendous tie-in because we in this country know that there is a dramatic correlation between poverty and demand for health care and the lack of health of individuals. We know that as the level of

poverty goes down, the higher the infant mortality rate is, the higher the rate of respiratory disease, the higher the rate of hospital admissions which cost us tremendous amounts in terms of health care. One of the things that this government has to realize is that if they are going to deal with the health status of Canadians, they must deal with the question of poverty.
Yet this budget slashes expenditures under the Canada Assistance Plan that are designed to deal with poverty and child welfare.
